 In a state which prides itself as fiercely independent – one-third of voters refuse to declare themselves a member of either party – his switching sides has not concerned people.
And indeed, independence is something his Republican rival is desperate to play up.
Donald Trump's approval ratings are at record lows, and so Collins is now doing her utmost to distance herself from her party's leader. She voted to impeach him in January 2021, and voted against some of his Cabinet members in both terms – notably Pete Hegseth and Kash Patel. But she did vote to confirm Robert F Kennedy Jr, and Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court.
She supported Trump's policies 95 percent of the time in 2025, according to CQ Roll Call analysis, and voted to advance the Big Beautiful Bill in the Senate, but then rejected it in the final vote – a classic, performative Collins move, her critics say. Her campaign insists it shows her independent streak.
Is it working?
'That's a great question, and in many ways the answer to it might be the biggest driver of the outcome,' said Professor Mark Brewer, chair of the University of Maine's department of political science.
'Collins has done a pretty good job of making the case, as she always does, for the benefits she brings to the state.
'Jackson has made a relatively strong case that Collins has changed over time, that she's become less bipartisan and less moderate.

'On the question of whether she's Trump's lackey, as Jackson wants to claim, or whether, as Collins claims, she's an independent voice who sometimes votes with the president when it's good for Maine and against him when it isn't, I don't know who's been more credible. But the answer to that would go a long way towards telling us who wins.'
Collins agreed to an unusual four debates with Jackson, in the hope that she could press home her independence, and stress her track record of using her powerful Senate appropriations committee position to help her constituents.
But her October 6 debate against Jackson saw her hand him perhaps the most powerful campaign slogan of the season.
'I have been strongly voting against the tariffs with Canada, but I've also been working behind the scenes,' said Collins. 'Troy mocked it, but I was successful in getting concrete pulp and road salt removed from the tariff list and if you ask towns in Northern Maine and Eastern Maine, they get all of their road salt from Canada.'
Jackson retorted: 'We can't eat road salt.'
His supporters have taken to wearing T-shirts emblazoned with the line.
So does the ghost of Graham Platner haunt Jackson's campaign? Or is it simply a referendum on Collins's five terms, and Trump's two?
Mike Hurley has lived in central Maine's Waldo County, a stone's throw from Platner's Blue Hill hometown, for over 50 years.

He told the Daily Mail that Platner's forced departure was 'painful' – but he was still supporting the Democrats.
'Susan Collins is on Team Trump,' he said, adding that he disagreed with the administration on 'a plethora of issues'.
Maine, sharing a 600-mile border with Canada, is hard hit by tariffs: only Alaska and Michigan share a longer landline with the northern neighbor.
Furthermore, it is a state strongly dependent on heating oil for homes – and the Iran war has sent costs rocketing. This time last year an average Mainer would spend $907 to fill their tank for the winter; today, the cost is $1,660.
'The tariffs and the war with Iran are huge issues for me,' said Hurley. 'And Trump turning on Ukraine is a terrible, terrible thing - and I don't hear Susan Collins saying anything about it. The country is going in the wrong direction, and I hope this turns it back.'

View gallery

Steve, a 40-year-old chef who has lived in the picturesque Bar Harbor area for ten years, is also voting Jackson, but is infuriated by the missteps that led to Platner's ouster.
'The Democrats are always trying to do the right thing, but they keep shooting themselves in the foot,' said Steve, dressed for work in his black chef's 'whites'.
He said he was dismayed by the 'clown show' of the Trump administration and Republican party, adding: 'These guys shouldn't be hard to beat.'
Indeed, this race is widely seen as the toughest of Collins's 30-year political career, and gives the Democrats their biggest chance in a generation of at long last turning New England entirely blue.
Collins is the last Republican standing in the region: the other 11 are all Democrat, except for the independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Angus King of Maine.
And yet Collins has, time and time again, proved herself to be remarkably resilient.
'I would never predict that Susan Collins is going to lose this race, because the Collins brand runs so deep in people's minds,' said Dr Brian Duff, an associate professor of political science at the University of New England in Maine.
'Collins has this brand in Maine that she's a moderate, that she's pragmatic, and that she works hard to deliver government contracts to Mainers and those sorts of benefits. She has been working to build that brand for a long, long time.
'But this president is the least popular any president has been going into a midterm in almost a century. It is really hard to run in that environment, even for someone like Susan Collins.'

news.title: Gas Attack: Blue States Have the Highest Prices at the Pump
news.text:
Democrats can't seem to decide whether they want higher or lower gas prices. On the one hand, they're promising that if they win a majority in Congress, they will work to bring down prices at the pump. On the other hand, they can't bring down prices in their own blue states.

 We at Unleash Prosperity recently analyzed gas and diesel prices in the 50 states. Here's what we found: The more Democratic a state, the higher the price of gas. For each additional percentage point of the state's vote that went to former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, gas prices are about 2 cents higher.

 On average, deep-blue states pay about 25 cents a gallon more for gas than deep-red states. Yes, we know correlation is not causation (umbrellas don't cause rain), but it does suggest that relying on Democrats to lower gas prices is probably a fool's errand.

 Take California, where gas now costs more than $6 a gallon. That's because of climate change policies and taxes that reach up to 75 cents a gallon. All told, Californians pay about $1.25 a gallon more than the average state. Yet California Gov. Gavin Newsom is considered a frontrunner for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028.

 Eight of the 10 states with the highest gas prices are run by Democrats. And eight of the 10 states with the lowest gas prices are run by Republicans.

 This isn't a coincidence. Democrats are so deeply in bed with the radical climate change lobby that they have done everything they can to strangle the industry. Let's not forget that one of former President Joe Biden's first actions in office was killing the Keystone XL pipeline.

 That was followed by a plan that his "climate justice agency" promoted, the goal of which was to stop all new production of fossil fuels. The plan was even opposed to nuclear power and aimed to curtail highway spending to discourage Americans from driving -- unless they were in an electric vehicle.

 New pipelines were to be banned.

 Meanwhile, several Democratic state attorneys general are suing the oil and gas companies for climate change costs. None of this is increasing our supply of oil.

 When President Donald Trump announced a "drill, baby, drill" energy dominance strategy, Democrats in Congress nearly had a cardiac arrest. Trump's energy policy has led to an all-time high U.S. output of oil and natural gas. How high would gas prices be today if we weren't now the world's leader in oil and gas? Anyone remember that former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi was in favor of natural gas until someone had to remind her that natural gas is a fossil fuel?

 America still gets the majority of its energy from the fossil fuels that the left hates: oil, gas and coal. To power the energy needed for the next tech revolution, we will need to double or triple our energy production, and it's a fantasy to think we can do that with windmills.

 As for gas prices, you can't in one breath talk about "net zero" carbon emissions and a war on our oil and gas producers and in the other breath promise lower gas prices at the pump.

 You don't send an arsonist to put out a fire.

news.text:
Wall Street Journal national security reporter Alex Ward says First Lady Melania Trump essentially stole credit for Pope Leo XIV’s hard work to broker a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia.

Hundreds of people from an occupied city of Oleshky, in southern Ukraine, were evacuated on Friday under a ceasefire agreement allegedly negotiated by Melania Trump, according to the White House. But Ward told “Today, Explained” co-host Sean Rameswaram that it was really the Pope who built the bones of the agreement.

“It’s possible she had a role. I’m going to personally, without too much reporting, say that it was probably more Pope Leo,” said Ward.

“Melania stole Pope Leo’s ceasefire?” asked Rameswaram.

“I think a little bit. … The Russians are very much saying, ‘look at Melania Trump, look at how important she was to all this.’ And if I’m the Russians, I would love to be saying things like that because then President Trump feels like the Russians are being very generous towards my wife and to my family, and therefore I side with them.”

“It feels very convenient that the Russians are pumping that up and that even the White House is pumping up Melania Trump’s influence,” said Ward, while adding that he did not want to fully discredit her. “I’m sure she did work on this.”

Ward added that while it’s “totally possible” that the First Lady is the driving force behind the ceasefire, he said “there’s just a lot of skepticism out there about whether Kyiv and Moscow were brought to the table and browbeaten by the First Lady.”

“Again, very possible, but both sides, being Ukraine and Russia, have an incentive to play up her role,” said Ward.

Meanwhile, Trump’s catholic approval has collapsed to 30 percent before the midterms, as Trump continues to square off against Leo and impose the White House’s will over the Hole See.

“Donald Trump won the Catholic vote in 2024 by twelve points, 55 percent to Kamala Harris’s 43 percent, reports Catholic Church correspondent Christopher Hale. And four years earlier, the same group had split almost evenly.

However, six days before the midterms, Pew now finds that only 30 percent of American Catholics approve of the job Trump is doing.

“For most of his first year back in office, the decline came gradually. Trump’s approval among Catholics fell to 42 percent by April 2025 and bounced around the low 40s through the summer and fall; by January 2026 it sat at 39 percent,” wrote Hale. “ … Since then, Trump’s Catholic approval has fallen another nine points, from 39 percent to 30. With white Catholics the slide runs steeper: 13 points, from 52 percent to 39, nearly double what he lost with them over his entire first year.”

Pew does not explain the collapse, but Hale said the slide has everything to do with another Trump-era war: his voluntary attack on Iran.

news.title: Hear me out: maybe Norway should give Melania Trump the Nobel peace prize | Arwa Mahdawi
news.text:
Haters be damned: Donald Trump just keeps on winning. He won the inaugural Fifa peace prize last year and was presented with the completely real, totally not made-up “Man of the Century” award at a recent rally. The president has also spent the greater part of a decade claiming he was once crowned Michigan’s Man of the Year: a fantastic achievement considering there is no such award and Trump has never lived in Michigan.

But despite his many trophies, there is one honour that has proved elusive: the Nobel peace prize. Trump holds a bit of a grudge about that, recently terming Norway a “shithouse country” for passing him over for the award. In response, the country’s tourism board highlighted some of its nicest public lavatories with the tagline: “Norway makes shit houses great again!”

Speaking in my capacity as Philadelphia’s Woman of the Millennium, I’ve got a modest proposal for the people of Norway. The toilet gag was excellent, but if they want to do some top-tier trolling then I think next year’s Nobel peace prize needs to go to Melania Trump.

Some people would be thrilled for their spouse to be in the spotlight, but I’m not sure that’s the case with Donald. Indeed, the president has said: “You can only have … one star in a family; it doesn’t work with two.” If Melania got Trump’s coveted Nobel peace prize, it could spark a war in the White House.

But look, I’m not just suggesting the Norwegians honour Melania because it would raise Donald’s blood pressure. No, it seems Melania has become quite the diplomat. Last week, the White House announced that the first lady had “successfully secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, localized to the city of Oleshky”.

How on earth did she manage that? Apparently, Melania initiated discussions with Russia and Ukraine and “aligned the parties on the agreement’s objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary”.

Whatever all that means, it seems to have worked: the ceasefire went into effect on Tuesday in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city, which has been enduring a worsening humanitarian crisis. On Friday, hundreds of people were evacuated from the frontline town and emergency supplies were brought in for people who needed to stay.

Melania has been widely praised for brokering this ceasefire. Melania’s adviser has claimed she “singlehandedly” secured it, adding that no other first lady has ever achieved what Melania just pulled off, and she is “completely revamping the role of first lady … [and] saving lives.”

Perhaps. But if there is one thing that the Trumps are good at it, it is taking credit for other people’s work. So is the first lady really the great peacemaker that she’s making herself out to be?

To be fair, Melania has done some good work vis-à-vis Ukraine and certainly seems to be better at peacemaking than Jared Kushner is, who has made huge sums of money while operating as one of Trump’s top diplomatic envoys to the Middle East. Last year, for example, Melania wrote a letter to Vladimir Putin pleading for Ukrainian children seized by Russia to be returned to their families. Since then, her office has said she’s facilitated numerous rounds of family reunification.

However, despite the claim that Melania “singlehandedly” secured this ceasefire, it would appear she had a little help. Pope Leo XIV also personally appealed to Putin about the situation in Oleshky in early October. It’s unclear whether he had more or less sway than the first lady had, but the pope is certainly being rather more modest about his involvement.

So what’s next for Melania after her success in Oleshky? In an interview with Newsmax, her adviser Marc Beckman said Melania might help pave the way to “durable, everlasting peace” in Ukraine and Russia as a whole.

“She’s against war, she thinks it’s senseless … she wants to see peace all over the world,” Beckman added.

Does she indeed? In that case she might want to have a word with the president, who started a very bloody war against Iran and who is currently trying to use US taxpayer money to send 2,000lb bombs to Israel, a country accused of genocide.

Forget the Nobel peace prize. If Melania can do something about her husband, I’m crowning her Michigan’s Woman of the Year.

Bad news for US women trying to manage menopause symptoms

Last November, the FDA announced that menopausal hormone therapy medications would no longer require a scary “black-box” label on them, which is the highest safety-related warning a medication can have. This reassured a lot of women about the treatment and caused a surge in demand. Supply didn’t keep up, and there’s been a shortage of estrogen patches in the US all year because of an uptick in demand. Now Reuters reports that the shortage has spread beyond estrogen patches “with some injectable and vaginal estrogen products also in short supply”.

Dolores Huerta, labor leader and civil rights champion, dies aged 96

Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers union (UFW), which improved conditions for agricultural workers in the 1960s and 1970s. She is also credited with coining the phrase “Sí, se puede!” (yes, we can), which was UFW’s slogan and then Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign rally cry.

Kamala Harris advises Democrats not to impeach Trump if they win House and Senate

“I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea,” Harris said in a MeidasTouch interview. “I was in the Senate for the last go-round, and the votes aren’t there.” In other words: don’t hold your breath that Trump will face immediate accountability if the Democrats dominate the midterms.

Egypt continues crackdown on press freedom and fines editor Lina Attalah

Attalah is the editor-in-chief of Madr Masar, an independent Egyptian news site that has frequently been critical of the Egyptian president Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi’s government. The government recently accused her of running a website without a license, detained her, and shut down Mada Masr. The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, one expert told the Guardian.

The toxic legacy of body positivity

“We are living through a strange time in the language around bodies,” writes Hannah Marriott in the Guardian. The body positivity era is over, but “much of its social training lingers.” Thanks to the GLP-1 boom, everyone is shrinking, but it’s taboo to talk about it. “What we’re left with is a world in which skinny bodies are lionized in fashion, culture and daily life, but to either admit a desire to conform, or express concern about it, feels socially verboten.”

Queer romance is dead: Chrishell Stause and G Flip have broken up

You may be familiar with this viral tweet: “I’m 50. All celebrity news looks like this: ‘Curtains for Zoosha? K-smog and Batboy caught flipping a grunt.’” I am still a mere 43, but I had my own curtains for Zoosha moment this week when I saw the headlines about G Flip, which I could have sworn was a watch. If you are similarly confused, Rebecca Shaw has an explainer as to why some of the queer community are in mourning.

 Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

news.title: Gavin Newsom touts ‘ruthless’ approach to politics in New Hampshire pitch
news.text:
The stated purpose of Newsom’s visit was to campaign for a slate of Democrats running in high-profile races for the House and Senate this fall and to help his party drive turnout. But it doubled as a way to test the waters for a presidential run that will require support in New Hampshire, a state that has for decades helped make or break the dreams of ambitious politicians like Newsom.

Being the governor of a liberal bastion like California has its downsides. GOP voters have a decidedly negative opinion of Newsom, thanks, in part, to years of cable TV punditry portraying him as a coastal elite, and at least some Democrats believe their party should look elsewhere if they hope to win in purple states.

“I mean, I love him. I think he’s wonderful,” said Denise Rudman, a retired high school teacher in Manchester. “There’s just something about, you know, ‘liberals from California,’ and I’m sure a lot of people feel the same way.”

Yet in the Trump era, Newsom is betting that “California” is anything but a dirty word and could actually differentiate him in a crowded primary field. At a town hall in Exeter, he quipped that he had just left the “most un-Trump state in the United States of America” as he opened his remarks.

“I say that with deep pride and privilege,” Newsom said.

Newsom’s notoriety as the governor of the biggest state in the country partially explains why he’s consistently ranked as one of the top contenders for the Democratic nomination in 2028. Polls show Newsom behind only former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2024 nominee.

He’s also a frequent target of the president, who has dubbed him “Newscum” and last year called for his arrest.

Newsom has played nice with Trump when California has needed federal relief, most recently with the Palisades wildfire, and insists that he’s “always had an open hand, not a closed fist.” But Newsom clearly relishes the confrontation and has returned the jabs with over-the-top mimicry on social media.

“We’re going to stand up and punch a bully in the mouth,” Newsom told reporters in Manchester. “This guy is — he’s the wrecking ball. What he’s doing in this country is jaw-dropping. There needs to be accountability, and we need to be tougher.”

That feud took on a new dimension this year when Newsom revealed that the Justice Department was investigating his wife over tax-related conduct, a step that he said amounted to political intimidation.

Newsom’s celebrity was apparent as he weaved his way through New Hampshire, now the third state on the Democratic presidential nominating calendar, shaking hands and posing for pictures with voters who stood in line for upward of 10 or 15 minutes.

At each event, his stump speech mentioned that Trump deployed the National Guard to Los Angeles first and continues to pick fights in court, most recently over California’s voter rolls.

“There will not be a fair and free election in the United States of America if we don’t take back the House of Representatives this year,” Newsom said. “We got to knock on those doors, we got to make those phone calls, we got to send those text messages out.”

Nancie Chandler, a finance manager from Derry, New Hampshire, said she thought that Newsom was knowledgeable and articulate about the stakes of the election and considered him a strong contender for president.

“He’s aware of what we’re going through, not only in New Hampshire or California, but really the whole of the country,” Chandler said.

Still, Newsom won’t have the anti-Trump lane to himself should he run next year, and he’s relatively untested outside of his home state.

Rudman, the retired high school teacher, said she preferred Pete Buttigieg, the former South Bend, Indiana, mayor who placed second in New Hampshire’s Democratic primary in 2020.

“He is thoughtful. He is eloquent,” Rudman said. “He’s brilliant, and he speaks for a lot of people.”

Other Democrats will gravitate to candidates who lack Newsom’s pragmatic streak and represent the party’s progressive wing. Despite its reputation for being a libertarian-leaning state, New Hampshire’s Democratic base has embraced left-wing politics, as evidenced by Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-VT) two primary wins there in 2016 and 2020.

Arya Shams, a candidate for state representative in Nashua, said he would like to see someone such as Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) or Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) run for president. Khanna, a Silicon Valley congressman, is running to the left of Newsom on a wealth tax that will appear on the California ballot in November.

“It’s nothing personal against Gavin Newsom, but Gavin Newsom is against some very important policies in his home state,” Shams said.

Newsom, asked what a post-Trump message might sound like after the midterm elections, leaned into economic populism, speaking of the need to “democratize our economy” and address the concentration of wealth and power.

As he finishes out his final year as governor, Newsom is also quick to put his record front and center and rattled off almost a dozen policies, from paid family leave to a higher minimum wage, with the speed of a fast-talking auctioneer.

“I’m practicing what I preach every day,” Newsom told the Washington Examiner. “I’ll go down the damn list.”

“We have painted our vision because I’m doing it every damn day, and I think that’s what we’ll all start to share,” he added.

news.title: Top Democrats are fighting a billionaire tax in California. Their voters are on the other side |
news.text:
Midway through this summer, a high-quality poll found that Democrats in California were overwhelmingly in favor of the upcoming ballot measure for a one-time 5% tax on billionaire wealth.

The ratio was more than 4 to 1. But the state’s most powerful Democrats – including the governor Gavin Newsom, his near-certain successor Xavier Becerra and the Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass – have lined up with Silicon Valley billionaires who’ve raised upward of $340m to defeat the initiative.

While Newsom has led the charge against the measure, most Democratic leaders in the deep-blue state have opted to duck. California’s senators Alex Padilla and Adam Schiff have stayed mum on Proposition 40. The same is true of the former vice-president Kamala Harris and the former House speaker Nancy Pelosi.

“Neither wants to alienate wealthy donors or their allies in labor by publicly opposing it,” the San Francisco Chronicle noted in mid-October. “But their silence on such a high-profile measure is giving cover to the billionaires” fighting the measure.

Nine-tenths of the billionaire tax revenue from Proposition 40 would go to healthcare for Californians in need. As the New York Times reported this month, “California stands to lose around $100 billion in federal Medicaid funding over the next five years, threatening healthcare coverage for millions of low-income residents, as well as the potential closure of hospitals and other facilities.”

With so much at stake in human terms, refusal to back Proposition 40 runs directly counter to standard rhetoric from Democratic politicians about standing up to the ultra-wealthy on behalf of the disadvantaged.

The stance of Newsom and other Democratic heavyweights in the state puts them on the side of billionaires in ongoing class war. The effect is that party leaders are offering a kinder, gentler oligarchy as an alternative to the far more corrupt Trumpist version.

Overall, a semblance of party unity has taken hold with the midterm elections looming. But clashes between corporate Democrats and progressives will soon begin to escalate.

The fact that the most prominent Democrats in the country’s most populous state are at loggerheads with the party’s grassroots on Prop 40 is a bad sign, but it’s hardly an anomaly.

Every time a general election nears, party leaders fervently call for a huge turnout – but their disconnect from the party’s base discourages turnout. California’s billionaire tax proposal is unprecedented, but the response to it from Democratic party elites is part of a pattern that has undermined capacities to build populist momentum against Republicans, let alone advance progressive agendas favored by voters.

Now being vilified by an onslaught of attack ads, Proposition 40 might get buried under the avalanche of billionaire cash (with nearly half coming from the Google co-founder Sergey Brin). The proposal’s foes have out-fundraised supporters by nearly 10-1.

But whatever the election’s outcome is on 3 November, campaigning to tax the wealth of the country’s nearly 1,000 billionaires has enormous potential nationwide.

In early August, the California Democratic Party executive board, hardly a bastion of class struggle, voted to give the party’s endorsement to Prop 40. But, undeterred, Newsom has gone all-out to fight the billionaire tax proposal as well as to boost another ballot measure that would nullify any such tax.

When I contacted a former chair of the state party’s Progressive Caucus, he was matter-of-fact about the alliance of big tech moguls with the current and next governor. “When it comes to Newsom and Becerra opposing the billionaire tax,” said Amar Shergill, a Sacramento-based attorney, “you need know only two things. First, Newsom needs billionaire money for his presidential campaign. Second, Becerra needs to pay back the billionaires that made him governor. The rest of the corporate Democrats in office are some version of these stories.”

Newsom became governor in 2019, following Jerry Brown’s second eight-year stretch in the job. His unique style aside, Brown has long been a kind of prototype for the state’s Democratic leadership now typified by Newsom.

“The way you have to approach the political process is something like piloting a canoe,” Brown said in 1979 during his first stint as governor. He explained: “If you paddle a little bit on the left side, then you paddle a little bit on the right side, you keep going right down the middle.”

This year, Brown has stayed out of the battle over Proposition 40. In late October, when I emailed the former governor to ask whether he supports it, he replied: “I have not discussed the proposition. There is already a plethora of opinions on the measure.”

Weeks ago, during a BBC interview, Brown lamented: “The gains for those who succeed at the top are getting bigger and richer, and the sustenance at the bottom and the middle is getting less and less.” He added: “We obviously need a wealth tax. If Tesla wants to give Elon Musk a trillion dollars over 10 years, then the people have to take back 99% of it. Now, can you get that? No, not at this point. Can you get it in one state? No, that would not work. Can you get it in one country? Probably not. So it would take an international agreement to tax the very wealthy, so that you can’t accumulate at the level that they are today.”

Brown and Newsom share a fondness for voicing lofty principles while kicking them very far down the road, tacitly equating deference to corporate power with realism. Newsom says – with scant details – that he would support a federal tax on billionaires. Meanwhile, he claims that approval of Proposition 40 would cause many of California’s more than 200 billionaires to move out of the state, with disastrous results.

“Proposed tax hikes on the rich invariably produce grim warnings of millionaire flight which then don’t eventuate,” the journalist Harold Meyerson recently pointed out. “Even if they did in this case, as a paper for the National Bureau of Economic Research has documented, the revenue gain of roughly $100 billion that the [billionaire] wealth tax would yield wouldn’t be offset by reductions in the income tax revenue produced by the flight of every one of those 200 billionaires until 25 years had passed. If just 50 of those 200 billionaires fled, it would take a full century.”

A large majority of the 45 Democrats in the California delegation to Congress richly deserve the “corporate” label. The official website of the Proposition 40 campaign lists only two congressional endorsers in the state. One of them, Representative Ro Khanna, has emerged as California’s most visible and vocal politician advocating for Prop 40.

“It’s the most important ballot initiative in America and in the world,” Khanna declared during a recent interview on MS Now. Looking ahead, he asked: “Are we going to continue to cater to a donor class that has hollowed out jobs, hollowed out the working class, and lost us two elections to Donald Trump?”

That kind of rhetorical question could progressively reframe the race for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028.

“This is a fight for the soul of the Democratic party,” Khanna told me last weekend. “Will we be beholden to billionaire donors and offer platitudes without policy like Gavin Newsom, or will we reclaim our FDR courage and offer a bold vision for our nation’s future?”

Exactly 90 years ago, speaking at Madison Square Garden on the last day of October 1936, the then president Franklin Delano Roosevelt scorned the rightwing plutocrats of the day: “They are unanimous in their hate for me – and I welcome their hatred.” Leaders of today’s Democratic party have failed to earn such hatred.

 Norman Solomon is the director of RootsAction and executive director of the Institute for Public Accuracy. His latest book is The Blue Road to Trump Hell: How Corporate Democrats Paved the Way for Autocracy

news.title: No matter what happens in the midterms, Canada-U.S. tensions are likely to remain
news.text:
DETROIT - Democrats are hoping Tuesday’s midterm elections will give them the power to rein in U.S. President Donald Trump — but Canadians hoping for an outcome that stabilizes the rocky bilateral relationship may be disappointed.

Once-safe Republican seats are now in peril and control of Congress could flip. Trump’s poll numbers are plummeting thanks to his unpopular war in Iran, rising energy prices and inflation.

Polling shows Democrats are favoured to take the House, where a net gain of three seats would give them a majority.

The future of the Senate is less clear. Democrats need a net gain of four seats for a majority, and some polling shows that is within reach.

Even if Democrats gain control of both chambers, Trump will still be president, said Matthew Lebo, a political-science professor at Western University in London, Ont.

Presidents have a lot of power over foreign policy and Trump — unhappy with being seen as a lame duck in the final stretch of his term — may be even more motivated to use it.

Lebo said that could make Trump more “erratic” and “dangerous.”

“It’s not clear how much the Democratic Senate will push back on him or can push back,” Lebo said.

The size of the expected Democrat win will be an important factor, Lebo added. Numerous reports suggest Republicans are worried about bleeding seats as contests in places Trump dominated in 2024, like Kansas and Ohio, become competitive.

Congress has control over tariffs and taxes but Republican lawmakers have largely given Trump a free hand to deploy tariffs worldwide. If the midterms demonstrate that the president has lost his hold over loyal voters, GOP members may be more inclined to break with Trump, Lebo said.

But a large number of Republicans would have to join with Democrats to secure the supermajority needed to bypass presidential veto power and overturn Trump’s tariffs.

And many observers question whether Democrats are looking to return to a pre-Trump era in trade policy.

Trump’s first administration demonstrated how vulnerable Canada is to American whims when the president scrapped the North American Free Trade Agreement.

It was replaced with the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, better known as CUSMA. Former Democrat vice-president Kamala Harris and current Democrat Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer were among the Democrats who voted against the trilateral agreement.

President Joe Biden brought more stability to the Canada-U.S. relationship but not much change. He kept many of Trump’s first term tariffs in place, despite promises to reverse them, and expanded other protectionist policies.

“What Canadians have learned in the last few years is we don’t trust Americans to correct course when they can in terms of the presidency,” Lebo said.

While Trump’s first term rattled the bilateral relationship, his second term blew it up. Canada was an early target of Trump’s tariffs and Canadians were shocked and appalled by the president’s repeated threats of annexation.

Tensions escalated further in August when trade talks collapsed. Trump slapped an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs, banned imports of other Canadian products and signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The trade war is deeply unpopular in states like Michigan and Maine, where tight Senate races ultimately could decide which party gains congressional control.

But even if Democrats emerge triumphant next week, or win the White House in 2028, it’s not clear that Trump’s tariff wall would suddenly drop.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is considering a run for president, told CTV in August that he couldn’t guarantee Trump’s tariff policies would be reversed under Democratic leadership.

One factor Democrats likely are considering is how to deal with the United States’ $40-trillion debt problem. Trump has argued tariffs bring in much-needed revenue — although they have yet to make much of a dent in the U.S. balance sheet. Democrats have not said how they plan to deal with the problem.

Vermont Democrat Sen. Peter Welch, who was in Montreal this week, vowed to repeal the tariffs on Canada.

Christopher Sands, director of Johns Hopkins University’s Center for Canadian Studies, said Democrats traditionally have been more protectionist than Republicans and he could see the party maintaining a baseline tariff wall.

What that means for the future of CUSMA is not clear. The Trump administration did not renew the trilateral agreement earlier this year, triggering an annual rolling review for up to 10 years. Once that period ends, and if the partners haven’t agreed to an extension at that point, the agreement would expire.

Sands said as long as the United States doesn’t walk away from CUSMA, there’s still room to negotiate.

“You just want to hang on to that and hope that in a different environment, you can have a conversation about keeping it,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 31, 2026.

news.title: Byron Donalds Could Become Florida’s First Black Governor. He Rarely Talks About It.
news.text:
MIAMI — Byron Donalds could make history on Tuesday. 

If he wins on Election Day, he’d become the first Black Republican governor of Florida — and the first Black Republican governor ever elected in the U.S. Only three Black governors have ever done so, and they’ve all been Democrats. 

“It can be very lonely sometimes,” he told HuffPost earlier this month, reflecting on what it’s like to run a gubernatorial campaign as arguably one of the most visible Black Republicans in politics. 

He had just left an event with the Jack Brewer Foundation, a conservative, faith-based nonprofit group in Miami’s historically Black neighborhood of Overtown. While there, he spoke to several young Black boys from the foundation — which mentors young people and works to combat fatherlessness, according to the group — about the importance of hard work and sacrifice to get ahead in life. 

While traveling with Donalds to his next campaign stop, HuffPost asked him whether he’d had a mentor of his own throughout his campaign. He paused for several seconds and glanced out the window. 

“Not really,” he finally said.

“I do know that I understand the gravity of what’s happening,” Donalds, 48, told HuffPost about his campaign. “A lot of perceptions, I think, of Black Republicans are kind of riding on what happens here.”

When Donalds first ran for Congress in 2020, he introduced himself in a campaign ad as “a strong, Trump-supporting, gun-owning, liberty-loving, pro-life, politically incorrect Black man.” He has since become one of President Donald Trump’s most reliable allies in the House and at one point was floated as a potential 2024 running mate. Donalds has Trump’s endorsement in this race, and received the support of outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis in September.

But as he crisscrosses Florida to court Black voters, a constituency that has seldom backed Republicans in large numbers, he is more measured in how he talks about his relationship with the president, whose approval ratings have hit a near-historic low. Trump’s rhetoric about Black Americans — from perpetuating the “birtherism” movement against former President Barack Obama, to casting doubt on then-Vice President Kamala Harris’ racial identity at a Black journalists’ convention in 2024, to frequently describing Black urban communities in 2016 as desolate, poverty-stricken or mired in crime — has drawn sustained criticism.

When questions around his loyalty to Trump do arise, Donalds is quick to push back on perceptions of his agenda as a proxy for Trump, casting himself as his own man despite consistently voting with Trump’s political agenda throughout his time in Congress. 

“With Black voters in particular, I think the first [misperception] is because I’m endorsed by President Trump, and that just means that I’m only going to do whatever he wants or whatever he says,” Donalds told reporters after a luncheon with Black men at a Caribbean restaurant in Florida earlier this month. “That’s not true. I have my own thoughts. I have my own opinions. I have my own ideas.”

But even at roundtables and community events aimed at Black professionals and entrepreneurs, Donalds has aligned with the Trump administration in a particularly notable way: He pitched his campaign message around “meritocracy” and his rejection of diversity, equity and inclusion — a position that has not landed with some. 

“To DEI, I’m going to be very clear. I’m not a supporter. I’m not a fan. I think it’s about merit and opportunity,” Donalds told a group of roughly 30 Black business leaders earlier this month at a private social club in Miami. 

The attendees began to glance at each other, shifting in their seats. There was no applause. 

“The way I move is, can you get the job done?” he added.

At a keynote event for Black professionals in Hollywood, Florida, the next day, he made the same case again, where some attendees in the crowd of roughly 100 murmured and sucked their teeth in response.

“As a Black man, there’s no way you can tell me that you don’t see DEI and equity and things of that nature being an issue,” said Levi Collins, 39, who was in the front row. “To get up there in a room full of Black professionals and try to run that game ... I think that’s where he lost the crowd.”

Donalds grew up in the working-class neighborhood of Crown Heights, Brooklyn, one of three children raised by a single mother who, in one of his campaign ads, says she worked two jobs to provide for her kids. He moved to attend Florida A&M University at age 17, and later graduated from Florida State University. 

He has described himself in his early 20s as “pretty lost,” addressing a period that included an arrest for possession of marijuana when he was 18. On the stump, he tells the story of how he became a Christian while working at a Cracker Barrel in Tallahassee at 21, and shares how he left the Democratic Party in 2010 to become involved in the Tea Party movement. From there, he worked his way from the Florida House of Representatives to Congress.

Since entering Congress in 2020, his voting record shows few breaks from his party’s right flank. Donalds holds a 97% lifetime score from Heritage Action, the conservative group that tracks how often members of Congress vote with its positions, including a 100% rating in the current Congress, compared with the average Republican score of 87%.

In the final sprint to Election Day, Donalds has blitzed across the Sunshine State to court Black voters, but it’s an uphill climb. According to an Oct. 28 New York Times/Siena College poll of all likely voters, Donalds is narrowly ahead of his Democratic opponent David Jolly by only four percentage points, 48% to 44%.

Roughly 10% of Black likely voters support Donalds, compared to 80% of Black likely voters who support Jolly, according to an Oct. 21 University of North Florida Public Opinion Research Lab poll.

A source familiar with the campaign who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy told HuffPost the campaign is aiming to win above 25% of the Black vote. 

If his support doesn’t improve, it would trail the roughly 13% of Black voters who backed DeSantis in his 2022 reelection bid, and 15% of Black voters in the state who supported Trump in the 2024 presidential election, according to CNN exit polling.

Steve Vancore, a longtime Florida pollster and political strategist, said the Donalds campaign goal faces long odds, in part due to the diverse bloc of voters within the Black community in Florida.

“The Black community is no longer as monolithic as it once was,” Vancore said. “Especially when you have Black communities that hail from the Caribbean. They don’t have the same world and life experience that other Black communities have.”

“It would stun me beyond belief if Byron Donalds got 20% of the Black vote,” he added.

The Republican Party, despite increasing the racial and ethnic diversity of candidates, has for decades struggled to reach and attract Black voters in high numbers in comparison to Democrats. A 2022 Pew Research Center analysis showed about 1 in 10 Black voters identified with or leaned toward the GOP.

While much can be attributed to policy priorities that misalign with the concerns of most Black Americans, Donalds acknowledged the outreach failures of his party.

“Democrats, they consistently are organizing in communities and having these conversations and these dialogues,” he said. “I disagree with their solutions. I disagree with their policy, but you have to recognize the reality that they continuously are in communities talking with voters.”

The Republican Party, he said, has treated Black voters as a short-term election-year exercise — a critique he has made before.

“I thought Republicans have gotten it wrong with Black voters for a long time. We have these conversations every election cycle where you just expect that, OK, we’re running, let’s do an African Americans for so-and-so coalition, and you did it for the election,” he said. “No, it’s [a] relationship over time… it’s not showing up for two months and thinking that you did something.”

His campaign’s most visible push to win over Black voters came earlier this month. After sparingly making his identity a piece of his pitch, Donalds’ campaign held a string of Black voter outreach events across Miami. The congressman held a forum at FAMU, his alma mater, where students grilled him, according to The New York Times. His team has rejected the idea that his Black voter outreach efforts are late, pointing to door-knocking teams and volunteers in Broward County and North Miami.

Before a drive to the next campaign stop in Orlando, Donalds was asked again about mentorship, and whether he wished he had a mentor in what is arguably the highest test of his political career. This time, his answers were more reflective.

“Yeah,” he said. “I’m breaking new ground here.”

He thought about it a moment longer.

The congressman had softly suggested he had less time for the role of a mentor in his personal life. The cost of his campaign has meant sacrificing the time available between him and the people closest to him, including with his three sons.

“Before politics, I spent a lot of time with my sons, coached them in sports, and that’s changed because of politics,” he said. “It’s really changed because of this campaign.” 

Whether it will be worth it on Nov. 3, Donalds said, “We’ll see.” 

He returned the question, this time considering his lofty goal ahead to become governor.

“I would assume if I’m successful here, I guess then would I become the mentor?” he wondered aloud. “It’s pretty crazy to think about, actually.”

news.title: The Midterm Billionaire War as America’s Oligarchs Pick Sides
news.text: Bernie Sanders had been railing against the billionaire class for years. In December 2010, the Vermont senator held the Senate floor for more than eight and a half hours to protest a bipartisan deal extending tax cuts for the wealthy. When he ran for president in 2016, it became a line in nearly every speech. Few in Washington paid attention to what he said. Polls showed that the billionaire class was not a big concern for voters, nor for Democrats. Gallup has long asked Americans to name the most important problem facing the country, and the gap between rich and poor drew roughly 2 percent of mentions, a number that hardly moved for over a decade. Democrats put it in a tie for ninth place as late as 2019. There was also the optimism of the Facebook years. Silicon Valley icons like Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, Jack Dorsey and many others were revered in pop culture, regular guests on talk shows and on magazine covers. Time named Zuckerberg its Person of the Year in 2010. Musk got the title in 2021, the same year he hosted Saturday Night Live. Gone are the years when tech tycoons were treated as heroes. America has soured on billionaires, and this election cycle, voters made sure politicians listened. Around 72 percent of Americans said there is too much money in politics, according to a Politico poll. Asked whether billionaires have too much influence, 61 percent said yes, including 75 percent of 2024 Kamala Harris voters and 55 percent of Donald Trump voters. In The Harris Poll's 2025 Americans and Billionaires Survey, 53 percent of Americans said billionaires threaten democracy, up seven points from the previous year. The amounts this cycle are unprecedented. Ad spending is projected to reach a record $11.6 billion, more than the $11.2 billion spent in the 2024 presidential race. Musk, the richest man in the world, has put $446 million of his own money into the midterms, most of it behind Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. Democrats have their own big donors. George Soros has given about $102 million this cycle. Michael Bloomberg added roughly $80 million in September and October. Reid Hoffman's money has gone to super PACs backing anti-billionaire candidates in Texas and Kentucky. In 2024, Kamala Harris's campaign spent about $1.5 billion over its 15-week run, close to $100 million a week in the busiest stretch. The argument Sanders made now has plenty of company. Robert Reich, who served as labor secretary under President Bill Clinton, wrote this week that billionaire wealth "becomes a public problem when it finds its way into politics — making it harder for average voters to be heard. It throttles democracy." Record Money After Citizens United As their involvement in politics became more public after the 2010 Citizens United decision, billions of dollars started pouring into political campaigns on both sides of the aisle. Under federal rules, an individual can give a candidate only $3,500 per election. After 2010, a super PAC backing that same candidate can take unlimited sums. This year, much of that money is going toward a defensive fight. Republicans hold both chambers in Congress and are trying to keep them with Trump's approval near historic lows. States the party once wrote off as safe have tightened, too. In late August, the Cook Political Report moved Iowa and Texas from lean Republican to toss-up, putting them alongside Alaska, Maine, Michigan and Ohio. Recent polling has shown Democrats ahead in Republican-held Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Kansas. "It just seems like the sentiment continues to go towards the Democrats at this point. The Republicans seem to have gotten a little bit of their footing. But there aren't too many people who are optimistic about them holding the line anywhere. It's just a matter of how bad it's going to be for them," Mike Madrid, a veteran Republican strategist, told Newsweek. The party's wealthiest backers have still answered with record sums. Of the $2.77 billion given by the 50 largest donors and organizations this cycle, Republican-aligned contributors account for $1.67 billion, twice the $832 million from Democratic-aligned ones, according to a Newsweek analysis of FEC records. Eight of the 10 biggest individual donors are on the Republican side. Soros and Bloomberg are the only exceptions. Musk tops the list. His $446 million is more than half of what every Democratic-aligned donor in the top 50 has given put together, and more than four times the Soros total. Democrats make up much of the difference through their own candidates. Looking only at money raised directly by campaigns, Democrats lead by about $285 million in House races and $425 million in Senate races. But once super PACs and other outside groups are included, the advantage flips, with Republicans holding a roughly $400 million lead, New York Times columnist David Wallace-Wells found, citing tabulations by political analyst Nate Silver. The split is easy to see in Texas. More than $367 million in ads have aired for Paxton, nearly three times what has been spent for Democrat James Talarico, according to figures released by AdImpact. Yet Talarico has raised about eight times as much as Paxton from donors giving to the campaigns themselves. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson brought in four times as much from Maine voters in the third quarter, but Republican Senator Susan Collins and her allies have outspent Jackson's side by 40 percent, Wallace-Wells wrote. Some of the biggest new players are less interested in which party wins than in what Congress does next. Andreessen Horowitz, the venture capital firm, spent barely $2 million on politics in the 2022 midterms. By May of this year, the firm and its founders had passed $115 million, much of it routed through super PACs that back friendly candidates in both parties: Fairshake for crypto, Leading the Future for artificial intelligence. OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, had added $50 million by the end of July. Crypto money has its own stars. Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss, the twins who fought Mark Zuckerberg over Facebook’s founding and were later portrayed in David Fincher's 2010 blockbuster The Social Network, had given $42.7 million by the end of July, mostly to Republicans, according to the Times. Billionaires vs. the Billionaire Tax The fight over billionaire money has also reached the ballot itself. In California, voters will decide Tuesday on Proposition 40, a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires who lived in the state on January 1, 2026. Most of the money would go to health care for low-income residents after federal Medicaid cuts. Emmanuel Saez, the UC Berkeley economist who co-wrote the measure, said it started as a request that billionaires "finally pay their fair share in taxes so that health care access could be preserved in California following Trump's Medicaid cuts." "Billionaires have spent huge ($300m and counting) to defeat it so Prop 40 has become the symbol of the battle between democracy and oligarchy," he told Newsweek. Google co-founder Sergey Brin leads the opposition with about $102 million. In December 2025, three weeks before the residency cutoff, he registered to vote in Nevada. Saez said the date was picked so billionaires would have a hard time leaving in time, since cutting tax residency also means cutting professional ties to the state. The New York Times has reported that Brin still commutes to Google in Silicon Valley every other week. "That means he is almost certainly liable for the wealth tax and that's why he is spending so much to defeat Prop 40," Saez said. Darien Shanske, a tax law professor at UC Davis who also helped draft the measure, doubted the move from the start. "The purported 'move' was never very plausible," he told Newsweek. The money has moved the polls. In September, 52 percent of likely voters backed the measure in a Public Policy Institute of California survey. By October, it was losing, 46 percent to 52 percent. Opponents also funded two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42. If either gets more votes than Proposition 40, the tax fails even if a majority approves it. Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff of SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the measure's lead sponsor, accused Brin and other billionaires of spending more than $1 million a day "to try to trick California voters." "The billionaires can buy all the ads they want," she said. "Billionaires can't buy the kind of credibility that our coalition members have with their members and communities, and they can't buy California voters." Saez expects the fight to outlast Tuesday regardless of the result. "Even if Prop 40 fails, the issue of extreme wealth concentration and the extreme power to influence society and politics that comes with it remains," he said. He predicted wealth tax proposals would surface in other states and be "front and center" in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary. Be Careful What You Wish For Sanders spent more than a decade railing against tax cuts for the rich, and for most of that time he was talking to himself. This year, Democrats from Texas to Maine are running on the same idea, though the party still depends on billionaires like Soros and Bloomberg to pay its bills. California shows how difficult that balance can be. Governor Gavin Newsom says he supports a national billionaire tax but opposes Proposition 40. On October 9, he endorsed Proposition 42, the countermeasure largely funded by Brin. Both candidates for governor, Republican Steve Hilton and Democrat Xavier Becerra, have also opposed Proposition 40. Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, said the party is walking a narrow path. "Democrats need to be cautious about courting billionaires," he told Newsweek. "In a populist moment and with the Democratic Party split on engagement, Party leaders will have to walk a fine line between policing business practices and continuing political funding from those with deep pockets." Others question whether the message wins votes at all. "It's fine for Democrats to take on the billionaire class, but don't expect it to win a whole lot of new votes," said Jim Kessler, co-founder of the centrist think tank Third Way. Democrats should focus on what makes "a material difference in the lives of ordinary people," he said, including taxing the wealthy "quite a bit more" if that's what it takes. "But just taking on the billionaires without handling people's daily concerns is not enough." Heidi Heitkamp, a former Democratic senator from North Dakota, sees voters' resentment as tied to technology. "When you're looking at the billionaire class today, those are the people who run technology in this country," she told Newsweek. She also warned the party against getting lost in big structural fights if it wins power. "If all they talk about is systemic change on, let's say, getting rid of monopolies or whatever that is, that's not gonna resonate with voters," she said. "Voters want an immediate kind of reaction and immediate policies that will alleviate their challenges when they look at their paycheck, and they look at their bills." The resentment has a MAGA wing, too, and its loudest voice has spent years fighting the richest man in the world. Steve Bannon, Trump's former White House chief strategist, started attacking what he calls the "oligarchs" before Trump's second inauguration. He splits them into Wall Street's "lords of easy money" and the tech titans of Silicon Valley, and he has called Musk "evil." The frustration shows up among Republican voters as well. A CNBC survey this month found that many Republican voters who back AI development oppose the data centers being built to power it in their own communities. You Can't Run From the Money There is also a contradiction. On the campaign trail, rivals have pounced on candidates who rally against the rich while taking their checks. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff calls the Trump White House "the most corrupt administration of all time." More than 70 billionaires have given almost half a million dollars to his campaigns, according to The Free Press. "The phoniest politician is a Democrat who whines about money in politics," Nathan Brand, a Republican strategist, told the outlet. At a rally in El Paso, Talarico said that "Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat." A super PAC supporting him has received money from Reid Hoffman and Adam Pritzker, and Bloomberg gave $2.5 million to another. Conservative critics have called him a hypocrite for it. Abdul El-Sayed, the progressive hopeful in Michigan, made getting money out of politics a pillar of his campaign. Then Senate Majority PAC, which received $9 million from Soros' Democracy PAC, committed $30 million to the state. After El-Sayed attended a fundraiser hosted by Soros' nephew, Republican Mike Rogers' campaign said El-Sayed was for money out of politics only when it wasn't being spent on him. El-Sayed has said he welcomes support from individuals who want to give. Hoffman also gave $500,000 in Kentucky to a super PAC backing Democrat Zach Dembo, who has campaigned against wealthy donors' influence. His Republican opponent, Ralph Alvarado, called it "dirty Epstein class money," a reference to Hoffman's past ties to Jeffrey Epstein. The sharpest exchange came in Maine. At a debate, Jackson told Collins that no billionaires were funding him. Two days later, his campaign report listed donations from at least four. "You said that you would take no money from billionaires. That's not accurate," Collins told him at their next debate. The state Republican Party chairman, Jim Deyermond, called it "blatant hypocrisy." Jackson's campaign says 95 percent of its contributions are under $100 and that it takes no corporate PAC money. Those small checks are up against sums that would have been hard to picture 16 years ago. In 2010, the year of the Citizens United decision, billionaires gave about $31 million to federal campaigns, less than 1 percent of all the money spent, according to Americans for Tax Fairness, a progressive advocacy group. This cycle, the group has already tracked more than $1.7 billion from billionaire families and the companies they control. Its count stops in August, before Musk sent another $158 million to Senate Republicans' main super PAC in September. The real number won't be known until well after Tuesday. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Voters have soured on billionaires. Candidates rail at them. And the billionaires are spending more than ever on the midterms.

news.title: How prediction markets harness the wisdom of crowds
news.text:
What are prediction markets?

Prediction markets are sites where users buy “yes” or “no” contracts on future real-world events. A contract pays $1 if it happens and $0 if not and its price is the implied probability.

Today, the biggest platforms are Kalshi and Polymarket. Both launched around the time of the pandemic but went mainstream during the 2024 US presidential race. In the week before that election, Kalshi processed around $750 million in trades.

Unlike a bookmaker, which sets the odds and takes the opposite side of every bet, prediction markets allow punters to trade against one another. You can bet on everything from the number of acres you think will get destroyed in wildfires and how often Donald Trump will say “Kamala” in a speech, to whether Jesus Christ will return this year.

Kalshi's valuation has quadrupled in under a year to £22 billion and has more than 10,000 live markets, although sport still makes up about 78% of volume.

Are prediction markets new?

The basic idea isn't. Americans have bet on elections since George Washington. However, the New York Stock Exchange banned such markets during Prohibition, when gambling flourished underground, and polling later replaced their use for predictive purposes. In 1988 the University of Iowa launched the first serious election market and developed a better record than Gallup at predicting future results. The non-profit PredictIt followed in 2014. Now polling is in crisis and the markets are back.

Who uses prediction markets?

Prediction markets are used by young men for the most part, says the BBC. According to Betterment, a US financial adviser, 52% of Gen Z investors diverted money intended for investment into sports betting last year. Firms target such investors through partnerships with celebrities and social-media accounts.

There have been attempts to court women too, considered more sceptical and risk-averse, by employing female “finfluencers”, hosting in-person events and offering bets on “female-friendly” topics such as pop culture. Kalshi told the BBC that women's share of its users rose from 13% to 26% between early 2025 and early this year.

It's not just a fad. Polymarket's boss, Shayne Coplan, calls his site a “global truth machine”, a nod to Friedrich Hayek's belief that markets aggregate dispersed, local and tacit knowledge better than any planner. Morgan Stanley found in August that Kalshi was more accurate at predicting CPI inflation than economist consensus forecasts compiled by Bloomberg.

This ability to harness the wisdom of crowds has seen Kalshi strike deals with CNBC, CNN and AP; Polymarket this year announced partnerships with Dow Jones and Substack.

Are people making money from prediction markets?

The founders pitch their platforms as being fairer than traditional bookies because there is no “house edge”. Polymarket and Kalshi together averaged some $1.6 billion of daily trading in August, up nearly 2,000% on a year earlier. Winning is another matter.

A study by the Centre for Economic Policy Research in June found that two-thirds of Polymarket users have lost money, with just 1% of profitable traders capturing more than three-quarters of profits, and 0.1% capturing half. The Wall Street Journal reported in May that nearly half a billion dollars went to fewer than 2,000 accounts, while the median loss last year was $94.

The reason is structural, says Jane McManus in The Guardian. The markets rely on “dumb money” users to supply the liquidity and mispriced odds that allow the “smart money” – professionals and increasingly AI tools – to take most of the profits.

Why do people still use prediction markets?

Ease is one reason. Prediction markets are always online, the financial commitment required is low, feedback is quick, positions are easily exited and – armed with AI tools – users can analyse markets themselves.

Other theories abound. Younger users have an underdeveloped pre-frontal cortex and a high appetite for risk. Other experts cite “financial nihilism”: the sense that the economy no longer rewards prudence or planning, and conventional pathways to wealth-building and stability have been cut off.

According to market researchers at The Harris Poll, nearly two-thirds of Gen Z and millennials think the only way to build wealth today is through gambling or crypto.

Aren't prediction markets illegal?

It's complicated. In the US, prediction markets are regulated not as gambling but as derivatives by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC). That lets them sidestep state bans on sports wagering and means the influencers they pay needn't mention risk. Both Kalshi and Polymarket emerged after the Supreme Court lifted the ban on sports betting in 2018.

Under Donald Trump, the CFTC has gone from “watchdog to cheerleader”, says The Economist. Trump wants prediction markets to thrive; his son Donald Jr advises Polymarket and holds stakes in both platforms. Europe is less welcoming. Across the continent, the platforms remain largely unauthorised and the EU's markets regulator has warned of significant risks and insider trading.

And in the UK?

Since 2019, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) regulator has barred the kind of binary options offered by Kalshi and Polymarket for UK customers and regulates prediction markets covering financial or certain climatic events.

Political and sporting outcomes fall to the Gambling Commission, which says they are “akin to” betting exchanges, a model Britain has allowed since 2000. Betfair, Matchbook and Smarkets are the legal versions.

Savvy Britons determined to bypass regulation are using VPNs to access Kalshi and Polymarket to place binary bets on such things as by-elections. But the situation may change. The platforms have begun a “lobbying blitz”, says the Financial Times, and hope soon to be regulated as financial services. The FCA is considering reforming its rules.

news.summary: Prediction markets have an enviable record of foresight when compared with experts and polling companies. But they can also be dangerous for the unwary
