news.title: America is starting to fight back against the Trump revolution
news.text:
This is Dispatches with Patrick Cockburn, a subscriber-only newsletter from The i Paper. If you’d like to get this direct to your inbox, every single week, you can sign up here.

Much of America views the congressional midterm elections on 3 November as judgement day for Donald Trump, when voters might give control of both houses of Congress to the Democrats and thereby hinder or cripple the President’s ability to do further evil to the world.

Trump was expected to do poorly in the midterms, as sitting presidents generally do. But it is his failing war against Iran, which is boosting prices and demolishing his reputation as a winner, that has done him what might just turn out to be fatal electoral damage.

If this is the case, we could be seeing the start of the unravelling of an extraordinary Trump-led counter-revolution which has sought to remake America in its own dark authoritarian image. For all his clowning and lies, Trumpism has the deadly serious purpose of transforming America as it was created by the Declaration of Independence in 1776, confirmed by the outcome of the Civil War (1861-65), and reinforced by the success of the New Deal in the 1930s.

Even Democratic optimists are nervous, as the possibility of the Republicans losing the Senate as well as the House is of very recent vintage. “If the election goes roughly as the polls say it will, then in some ways it would mark the end of the Trump era,” premier election forecaster Nate Silver told Ezra Klein of The New York Times. “If Trump has a bad night, as polls show, then he’s a super-lame duck.” 

Not only will he be hampered and harassed by a vengeful Democratic majority in Congress, but power automatically drains away from a sitting president during his last two years in office as focus shifts to his potential successors.

It is the US-Israeli war on Iran that has made all the difference. A year ago, rising prices were damaging Trump. He himself said it after the 2024 election: “I won on the border” – that is, immigration – “and I won on groceries”, meaning prices. 

Price inflation has continued to soar, but today the higher cost of fuel can be attributed entirely to Trump’s decision to attack Iran on 28 February. American voters almost always punish parties that engage them in foreign wars, so it is scarcely surprising if they blame Trump for a debacle that has left the much demonised Iranians and Houthis in Yemen strategically stronger than they were before the conflict.

Trump’s strength in the past was that he had fanatical core support – the so-called Maga base – but he also could assemble an electoral coalition broader than the traditional Republican reach. Barack Obama had been able to do the same for the Democrats. Most of the male white Trump fundamentalists remain on board, but it is his old coalition that has fragmented. Hispanics and young people, traditional Democratic voter cohorts who had rallied to Trump in surprising numbers in 2024, are massively redefecting, according to the polls.

Republican candidates who once piously invoked Trump’s name in their speeches to their electoral advantage today fear he has become a vote loser. In heavily Hispanic South Texas, an area with a population of 1.5 million, this Republican bid to play down the Trump connection has provoked a strange row. 

This revolves around roadside billboards featuring a picture of the Republican House candidate, Eric Flores, standing beside Trump topped by the words “Trump Endorsed” and below the words “Support ICE!”. Only those who get close will see in smaller letters the message that this piece of political advertising is paid for the local Democratic Party organisation, which calculates that Trump’s name is now toxic among Hispanics, who make up almost a third of the Texas electorate. The Republican campaign has sent a cease-and-desist letter to the Democrats demanding that the billboards be removed.

Sceptics argue that whatever setbacks are suffered by Trump, he will carry on regardless and simply ignore a hostile Congress. Conceivably he will even begin a third round in his war against Iran in alliance with Israel. But like Shakespeare’s King Lear, he may find that it is not only Republican candidates in South Texas who have a much less compliant attitude to rulers in decline than in the ascendant. 

Last year there was a huge and shameful capitulation of powerful individuals and institutions to a triumphant Trump, as he hacked away at the foundations of American democracy. The notorious War of Independence traitor Benedict Arnold, who sought to betray his side to the British, used to be held up to American schoolchildren as the worst of unpatriotic side-changers. But the first year of Trump’s second term saw gaggles of modern day Benedict Arnolds – from business, academia, military, judiciary, media and beyond – bend the knee to a quasi-monarchical Trump and switch to what they believed was the winning side.

It would be deeply gratifying if all these capitulators and collaborators with Trumpism turn out to have bet on the wrong horse, though this might also be wishful thinking. One descriptive term for Trumpism is plutopopulism, and while Trump may be losing some of his popular appeal, he still has the backing of vastly wealthy plutocrats. 

By late October, Elon Musk alone had contributed $445m (£332m) to the Republican Party at the local and federal levels. Massive donations do not automatically turn into votes, but they do help and might be enough to prevent a Republican wipeout.

Against this, the Democrats this time around are fielding many candidates who know how to make a speech, in contrast to the moribund and incoherent President Joe Biden and his uninspiring vice president – and the eventual Democratic presidential candidate – Kamala Harris.

This time around it is encouragingly different. More Democratic politicians know how to throw a rhetorical punch which connects with the target. This matters more than 30 years ago because speeches can be watched by hundreds of thousands, if not millions, on YouTube and other platforms. This may be one reason why Democrats are at last cutting through and making charges of alleged corruption stick against the Trump administration. 

Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff is a good example of this, telling an audience: “They promised to drain the swamp. Instead, it’s the most corrupt administration of all time, and everybody knows it. And while the crook President and his crook family rake in billions from all over the world, you pay more for everything. They doubled your insurance premiums and slashed Medicaid to cut taxes for the rich.”

This is rough but effective stuff. Possibly we are about to see the poisonous Trump tide recede to the benefit of Americans and the world at large. But not all arrows point in the same direction. 

Suppose, despite the forever wars Trump promised not to wage and the corruption lapping through the doors of the White House, he remains in the ascendant. What does that say about Americans and America – and the future of the planet?

Further thoughts

I am depressed but not surprised that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu outperformed the opinion polls and survived the general election on 27 October. Survival was all he needed to do, since he remains caretaker prime minister and, though his coalition bloc has lost its majority, he stands a good chance of rebuilding it through defections from a fragmented opposition or a unity government under his leadership.

His winning formula is the same as ever, which is to exploit Israelis’ fear of Palestinians at home and Arabs and Iranians abroad. The slogan of his Likud party in this election was “The Right or Palestine”. Israelis’ sense of insecurity has always been high and is higher than ever because of Hamas killing 1,200 Israelis on 7 October, 2023. This combines with the last round of the war with Iran earlier this year, when Iranian missiles were exploding everywhere and Israelis had to retreat to bomb shelters night after night.

Netanyahu’s strategy of no compromise with the Palestinians, or anybody else for that matter, has served him well for the last 30 years because it guarantees never-ending Israeli insecurity of which he is the political beneficiary. 

His message to Israelis has always been that the Palestinian can be either ignored or utterly defeated, though his own career indicates the falsehood of this belief. First elected prime minister in 1996, he effectively ran against the compromise with the Palestinians embodied in the Oslo Accords. The door to power opened to him when Israeli prime minister Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated by an opponent of Oslo as he left a peace rally in Tel Aviv in 1995. 

Yet, although Netanyahu has been prime minister of Israel for 18 of the last 30 years, the Palestinian issue has remained stubbornly at the heart of Israeli politics despite his efforts to marginalise them. His winner-takes-all policy has provoked escalating and unresolved crises at home and abroad.

Demonising the 2.1 million Palestinians who make up 21 per cent of Israel’s population has the practical advantage of ejecting them as players in the formation of the next Israeli government. They voted in unprecedented numbers in the election, winning 19 of the 120 Knesset seats, which means that 67 Knesset members just elected won on an anti-Netanyahu platform. Yet it is not only Netanyahu but the opposition who treat these Israeli citizens as political pariahs. As Haaretz puts it, the opposition chiefs nearly all “capitulated to Netanyahu’s fear-mongering campaign against the Arab-led parties, vowing not to join with the only force that could help them defeat him”.

The opposition to Netanyahu is a rag-bag of discordant parties and factions often led by opportunist leaders, so an Israeli who feels unsafe has every reason to opt for Netanyahu as a known quantity and a strong leader. Moreover, the opposition have no real-world alternative policies on key issues like Israeli relations with Palestinians and the war with Iran. The only glue holding them together is hatred of Netanyahu – and that was not enough on election day.

Netanyahu’s endorsement by Trump pushed up his support because Israelis know how much they depend on full American backing – and this dependence is greater than ever.

Over the years, Netanyahu’s toxic version of Israeli nationalism has progressively poisoned the Israeli body politic at every level to the point where recovery may be impossible. This election just might have been a turning point, but all the signs are that it was not.

Below the radar

I have long believed that selectivity in war reporting is more harmful and effective than fake facts and propaganda when it comes to misleading us about what is really going on.

Nevertheless, it came as something of a shock this week to realise that the Black Sea, one of the world’s great trade routes, is today more dangerous for ships and their crews than the Strait of Hormuz. 

Since midsummer, Ukraine and Russia have engaged in swiftly escalating attacks on ships with drones and missiles that has largely stopped Ukraine’s once huge agricultural exports and Russia’s oil and grain exports through the Black Sea. Port facilities in and around Odesa in south Ukraine that once handled five million tonnes of grain exports a year are closed.

The media discovered the importance of the Strait of Hormuz earlier this year and speak of it continually, but the Black Sea gets scarcely a mention. Shippers may risk vessels in the Strait of Hormuz because freight rates and profits are high but not in the Black Sea where they are lower. Their view of the dangers involved is shared by insurance underwriters who told the Financial Times that war risk insurance for vessels in the Black Sea was 15 per cent of hull value, twice the rate they charge for the Strait of Hormuz.

If shippers continue to operate at all in the Black Sea, they use older and less valuable vessels. The sea war has spread down the west side of the Black Sea to the Danube river ports with ships in waters off Romania and Bulgaria also being hit and, on occasion, sunk.

Cockburn’s picks

There is a mountain of reporting, analysis and commentary about the state of America in the run-up to the midterms, but I found a lengthy essay entitled “Another Country” by Adam Shatz in the London Review of Books from earlier this year the most clear-eyed and perceptive account of the great American crisis that I have read anywhere.

news.title: After the Midterms, Will Progressives Break the Electrical Grid?
news.text:
During Joe Biden’s disastrous four years as acting President, ruled by puppet masters, we witnessed massive airline transportation boondoggles; toxic train derailments, a curious string of facility-destroying fires at large-scale food processing plants, nationwide baby formula shortages, blatant crime sprees in all major Democrat-run cities, 10+ million illegal aliens flooding our borders, and free healthcare and relocation for such illegals.

We also witnessed major military bungles in Afghanistan and elsewhere, military wonkiness over defense preparedness, nuclear weapons brinkmanship, out-of-control funding for Ukraine, a major Middle East flare-up, a plethora of Chinese spy balloons traversing the U.S., intensified weaponization of the DOJ and the FBI, the persecution of political enemies, runaway inflation, and depletion of our strategic energy reserves, not to mention so much more that was totally undesirable.

As happened in über-progressive California, when an epic heat wave in the summer of 2022 nearly brought the state’s power grid perilously close to collapsing, it was only natural to contemplate, among endless ‘progressive’ blunders, when would major components of the national electrical system fail?

Actor Dennis Quaid produced a documentary showing how everything from terrorist or anarchist attacks on power stations, to weaponized Chinese balloons, to atmospheric anomalies, to overgrown tree limbs could revert us to the 1880s with implications far more severe than the height of COVID. All of which reminds me of November 1965.

Déjà Vu All Over Again

One afternoon after school, I accompanied my father, a vice principal in Hartford, CT, who served as head lifeguard at an indoor pool. It was totally cool for me to have the run of the pool as I so often did.

I was in the lifeguard office playing around with the lights a few minutes before half past five, while my father was watching the pool several dozen yards around the corner. One of my juvenile games back then was to flip the lights on and off so quickly that no one in the pool could tell that anyone had tampered with the lights.

My father was a sharp cookie; however, he called out from afar, “Jeff, stop playing with the lights,” and I did at once.

Now, the Real Fun

No more than 60 seconds later, the lights went off in the entire pool area and only one small light from an independent power generator was illuminated. My father spoke up again, “I told you to stop playing with the lights.” I came out of the office door and looked down the length of the pool. I said, “It wasn’t me.”

We looked outside at the parking lot and saw that no lights were on. I opened the door and looked at the rest of the facilities, and all of the lights were off except for some small lights, once again, powered by emergency generators.

The lights remained off for several more minutes, and my father had no choice but to close the pool. We found some flashlights and ushered swimmers into the locker rooms. Other staff from around the center assisted people in gathering up their belongings and exiting the building.

'A Dark and Dreary Night'

On the drive home, we noticed that all streetlights in West Hartford and Bloomfield, and all lights that we normally would see from houses along our route, were also off. The car radio was working, and we learned from a local station that the entire metro area, and perhaps the whole region, had no electricity.

As we arrived home, we heard a newscast: the entire Northeast had gone dark. Later, it was determined that the electrical failure was due to an over-extended, protective relay device near Niagara Falls in New York; in other words, nowhere near us! This was the Great Northeast Blackout of 1965 — a U.S. first-time event, and it was stunning. Until then, flipping on the light switch always resulted in your lights coming on.

During the blackout, families retrieved flashlights, candles, and transistor radios. They made their homes as comfortable as possible. It wasn’t too cold that November evening, so most places in our geographic region were okay.

With no television, people listened to the radio, took walks, or camped around the kitchen table and devoured what they could before their food spoiled.

Larger Forces at Play

Today, I remember my father directing me for a second time not to play with the lights when, indeed, larger forces were at play!

How long before the electrical grids in some parts of the country (hint: blue states) go haywire? If Kamala Harris had been elected, given the Biden administration’s ineptitude, and assessing that she wouldn’t change a thing that their Administration did, it was only a matter of time.

In California, today, such issues are ever-present. With the Trump administration’s approach to energy management and protecting the national power grid, when you flip on the light switch, guess what? The lights go on. Just in case, buy a lot of candles right before the midterm elections in case the wrong people get into office, and before the November 7, 2028 presidential election; it’s difficult to read in the dark.

news.title: Why voters won't reject Netanyahu
news.text: For a decade, “friends” Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu have vied for the top spot on the hate list for Westernised liberals and the Left. Their political demise has been foreseen and wished for. Both keep disappointing their haters. Mr Trump won the presidency twice, riding liberal ridicule and contempt. Mr Netanyahu has turned that knife for 16 of the last 17 years, barring the 2021-22 Naftali Bennett-Yair Lapid interruption. This week, he pushed the knife deeper. He hasn’t secured another mandate. But he has the highest tally, support of the hard-Right. He’s better placed to build a coalition. Or, he can orchestrate a fresh election, not unfamiliar in Israel. Mr Netanyahu has won only because he hasn’t been defeated. He’s also changed Israel fundamentally, with some “help” from Hamas. In another world, it might’ve been possible for rival Gadi Eisenkot to expand his coalition from 48 seats to beyond the 61 needed for a majority by aligning with the two Arab parties. After all, one of them, Ra’am, had joined Bennett-Lapid’s short-lived coalition in 2021-22. But now, no Jewish group can embrace the Arabs unless they condemn Hamas as terrorists. And Arab parties won’t and can’t do that. It will have to be a coalition to the exclusion of Israel’s Arab citizens. That’s how Mr Netanyahu and Hamas have changed Israel. There’s no “middle” left in Israel. In the US, the Democrats may restore some balance in the midterms next week, but that won’t change the reality of what rocketed Donald Trump to imperial power. His impact on immigration, trade, and human rights will endure long after him. To understand the Trump-Netanyahu phenomenon we must accept that the voters are emotional, yet rational. They’re also more transactional than ideological. And what’s the “deal” they want? The economy matters, but three things take precedence: National security, individual safety and preservation of identity. In America, Mr Trump made his second election about law and order, immigration, and “over-the-top” political correctness — DEI (diversity, equity and inclusion) overhang in academia, gender fluidity, and open borders. Two eruptions — Black Lives Matter, and the fury on liberal campuses over Gaza — gave him tailwinds. The question then: Who could White Americans and many Hispanics trust on these issues? Mr Trump or Kamala Harris? Compared to security, safety, and identity, other concerns become softer, dispensable. Israel is an ongoing story. They had a single-point, national-security election. For them, October 7, 2023, was their most traumatic experience since the Holocaust. Further, over the past three decades, the Iranians have encircled them with their “ring of fire”, or the “axis of resistance”. Israelis are inured to endemic fighting. But October 7 was a devastating defeat. For the first time, large Jewish populations in the Israeli heartland found themselves incapable of defending themselves. This changed Israel, built support for the wars that followed, and protected Mr Netanyahu from anti-incumbency. Contrary to stereotypes that dominate liberal debate in democracies, including India, Israelis have a deep, argumentative, and democratic tradition. There exists a strong, liberal, and vocal constituency that’s sympathetic to Palestinians, abhors settler violence in the West Bank, and even supports the two-state idea. The one Israeli newspaper I’ve subscribed to for years is Haaretz, and it’s way to the Left of anything mainstream in India. It has been deeply critical of Mr Netanyahu, and has broken stories that should have devastated him politically. These include how he ignored warnings from Egypt and the UAE before October 7. It’s also been widely insinuated that he deliberately ignored these. Conspiracy theorising isn’t alien to the Israeli debate. At the other end are ultra-orthodox parties who want to evict all Palestinians from the West Bank and Gaza. In short, there are deep disagreements in Israeli society, and idol worship doesn’t come naturally to it. There isn’t any for Mr Netanyahu either. That these divisions didn’t play out in the vote is the important point. Jews chose between one hardliner or the other. The 21 per cent Arab minority, in the proportional voting system, does get seats but its votes ultimately don’t count as the majority consolidates for safety and survival. The question was simple. Who can we trust more with protecting us as we pass through a frightfully insecure era: A known devil, or his adversary, who’s no dove either? Mr Netanyahu had appointed General Gadi Eisenkot as IDF chief; Eisenkot’s soldier-son died fighting in Gaza; and he’s also committed to wiping out Hamas. Enough people voted for continuity, than risk change. Two points need exploration. One, when and why did the power of the once-formidable Left vapourise in Israel? And second, how come the formidable vote of its Arabs doesn’t matter? The era of Left (Labour) domination in Israel isn’t widely remembered in India. David Ben-Gurion, Golda Meir, Levi Eshkol, and Yitzhak Rabin —the greatest Zionists and founders of the modern state of Israel — were all from Labour. The legendary Lt-General Moshe Dayan was a Labour socialist and a self-declared Zionist-atheist. He left Labour to support Menachem Begin’s Likud coalition as foreign minister in 1977 to negotiate the Camp David Accords for peace with Egypt. From 1948 to 1977, Labour domination was total, until Begin’s Likud broke it. Under Shimon Peres, Rabin and Ehud Barak, Labour returned for short spells—in 1984, 1992, 1995 and 1999—and then faded. Labour, in the 1992-2000 period pushed for Egypt-like peace through the Oslo Accords negotiations and failed, amid rising Palestinian attacks and suicide bombings. The first time, it ended with Rabin’s assassination; then in 2000, as the Second Intifada became imminent. Ultimately, the Israelis saw Labour’s idea of trading land for peace as woolly-headed. They killed it, burying Labour with it. It’s since been impossible in Israel to seek votes for peace. Ironically, while most countries, India included, keep supporting a two-state solution, neither of the two direct antagonists wants it. Both Israelis and Palestinians want a single state, with each seeking to drive out the other. Each has its version of “from the river to the sea”. The Palestinian movement lost its socialist-secular-Christian appeal. It’s now Islamised. This is Iran’s leverage, and ideological fuel for its proxies. And the second point, why the Arab vote has become so inconsequential. We need to study it closely because lately there’s been some clamour for proportional voting in India instead of the first-past-the-post system. That way, it’s believed, minority seats would reflect their population. Israel provides a rude reality check. The mostly Muslims Arabs account for more than 20 per cent of Israel’s population, work in the government, businesses, and even the armed forces, though they are exempt from conscription. They just secured a record vote, translating into 19 seats in a Knesset of 120. They can be kingmakers, but nobody will touch them. In the broader Israeli picture, they fail the test of nationalism. One group, with 11 seats, was reported to have celebrated with Palestinian symbolism at its headquarters in Nazareth. They “condemn” October 7, but won’t call it terrorism or refer to Hamas as terrorists. No Jewish party will embrace them. Their numbers become inconsequential. See it like this. If you switched to proportional voting in India and Muslim parties won seats equivalent to their population (about 80 of 543), would even a “secular” coalition accept them if, heaven forbid, they celebrated with Pakistani or Hurriyat flags or symbolisms? Or refused to call Lashkar and Jaish terrorists? I know many will be outraged by this suggestion. But see how careful and correct Asaduddin Owaisi is. I use this example only to underline how the Israelis feel about their Arab parties. This is a lesson for minorities in any electoral democracy. They gain very little by isolating themselves. They have to ally with enough of those in the mainstream whom they find acceptable, and stitch a coalition. It needs ideological compromise and uncompromising nationalism. That’s how the Muslim vote acquired power in India in the 25-year coalition era (1989-2014). Or, you can campaign for proportional representation and collect numbers but be marginalised, like the Israeli Arabs.By special arrangement with ThePrint

news.title: ‘The View’ co-hosts say Dems shouldn’t impeach Trump if they regain control of Congress
news.text:
“The View” co-hosts agreed with former Vice President Kamala Harris Friday that impeachment would not be a good use of the Democratic Party’s time and resources if the party wins back control of Congress in the midterm elections.

“I think that going on in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea,” Harris warned Tuesday on “The Parnas Perspective” podcast. “OK, just to be honest with you. Because we have limited resources, and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations. And that’s where the time should be spent. Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-round and the votes aren’t there, right? So, that’s how I feel.”

After playing a clip of Harris’ comments, “The View” co-hosts agreed with her assessment.

“In terms of Trump, no, I don’t think that’s what should be on the agenda,” co-host Sunny Hostin said. “Hakeem Jeffries — who I believe will be the next speaker of the House, after November — he has a plan for 100 days which includes tax credits, taking care of the tax credits, limiting ICE and also stock trades. 

“And then he’s got a plan for the first 100 hours, which would include, you know, just undoing a lot of unpopular Trump policies. So, I think there is a plan in place that Democrats have, and it may not include impeaching Trump.”

“I think that Democrats have to be realistic of what’s achievable,” co-host Ana Navarro said. “We are four days away from the election. So, before we start talking about what Democrats are going to do once they win, they’ve got to make sure they win. 

“People have to focus not on all of the conversation about impeachment and what is going to happen but rather on getting out the vote and getting people to the polls so that the American people decide who they want in power in the House and in the Senate.

“There’s a limit to what Democrats are going to be able to do even if they win the House, even if they win the House and the Senate, because Donald Trump is still president,” she continued. “Legislation in this country needs to be signed by the president. If not, it needs to have a veto-proof majority. And I think that’s going to be very difficult to achieve. I’m completely against impeachment.

“There’s 100 other ways to hold Donald Trump and his administration accountable,” Navarro added. “Impeachment is an exercise that’s moot if you don’t have the 67 votes in the Senate required to indict.”

Joy Behar pointed to former President Richard Nixon’s resignation from office after Republican lawmakers warned him that he lacked sufficient Senate support to avoid conviction if impeached and said of Trump, “If we don’t have the votes to convict, there’s no point in impeaching.”

Sara Haines also agreed, arguing that many of Trump’s supporters are now angry with him for breaking campaign promises and that Democrats could capitalize on their dissatisfaction by delivering on their own promises.

“It’s important to recognize the moment,” she said. “Donald Trump was elected and promised things he never touched. He’s been remodeling, redecorating, working to revenge, all the things. The voters were left high and dry, which is why we’re seeing some red states flip full to blue,” she said. “That’s why we are watching this campaigning.

“They need to see someone get in there, hold them accountable, do the investigations, fine,” Haines continued. “But really show the American people that what they promised, to fix all these things, that immediately there’s action taken. Even if it can’t get past the president. Spin the wheels. Show the people that you are putting up policy, that you are taking things to vote, that you are actually acting for the people that put you there.”

“Impeachment is not where the focus should be,” Alyssa Farah Griffin said. “It costs actually a lot of money to do a trial, do the investigation.

“What I think is important is there are day one things that would be beneficial for all Americans and a lot of Republicans would be on board with that a Democratic Congress could do,” she continued.

“Repealing Trump’s tariffs, that is the power of the purse controlled by Congress and trying to wind down or pause the war in Iran. Those are things you should get Republican votes to do. That will bring down people’s fuel prices. Those are where the focus should be.”

Earlier this month, veteran Democratic strategist James Carville also warned Democrats against impeaching Trump if the party wins control of Congress in the midterms.

Democratic strategist and co-host of “The Huddle” podcast Dan Turrentine told Fox News Digital, “Neither the Senate arithmetic nor the American people are there. Folks are angry with the president about the economy, tariffs, healthcare, the war with Iran, corruption. They feel he is focused on everything but them.

“Our job is to fight for the real lives of real people, solving their problems, while providing appropriate oversight of the executive branch and trusting the electorate provides accountability,” he added. 

“The quickest path back to the minority or continuing to be on the outside, looking into the White House, is to focus on revenge and score settling.”
news.summary: "The View" co-hosts agreed with Kamala Harris that Democrats should focus on policy and investigations rather than impeaching President Donald Trump.
news.author: Fox News

news.title: Exclusive: ‘Republicans’ Backing Talarico, Trone Garriott Have Histories of Supporting Democrats
news.text:
Democratic U.S. Senate and House candidates in Texas and Iowa are highlighting endorsements from self-described Republicans in the final days before the midterm elections, but voting and campaign finance records obtained by Breitbart News reveal that several of those supporters have previously participated in Democratic primaries, donated to Democratic candidates, or publicly endorsed Democrats in earlier elections.

Texas Democrat James Talarico, who is running against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton for the U.S. Senate, recently launched a “Republicans Pass on Paxton” campaign featuring five former Republican elected officials endorsing his candidacy.

The advertisement opens with the men identifying themselves as Republicans and declaring that they are “passing on Paxton.”

“I truly believe that he is the most corrupt politician Texas has ever seen,” former Tarrant County Judge Glen Whitley said.

“Ken Paxton is just far too corrupt for Texas,” former Republican Rep. Alan Steelman said.

Former Ennis Mayor Russell Thomas said, “You know where Ken Paxton has been. Ken Paxton has been in court. He’s been impeached by his own party.”

“I’m ashamed that Ken Paxton is even on the ballot,” Whitley added.

The former officials also expressed their support for Talarico, with former Texas State Rep. Bennett Ratliff declaring, “James Talarico is by far, without a doubt, the best person in the race for the U.S. Senate.”

Former Texas State Rep. Todd Smith described Talarico as “extremely genuine” and “a person of very high moral character.”

“James hears us. He sees us. He will be our eyes and ears in Washington. He will be our voice,” Steelman said.

“We don’t always agree, but he’s willing to have an open dialog and hear my side,” Ratliff said.

“The idea that half of the American people are wrong all the time is just false,” Smith said. “And the first thing we need to have is a representative that understands that fundamental fact, and I have no doubt that James Talarico is in that category.”

“I’m a lifelong Republican, and I know it’s hard to go in and vote for a Democrat,” Whitley said.

“We must remember that how we vote says more about us than it does about the candidate on the ballot,” Steelman added.

“We need to support the best person, not look at their party label, not look at what Jersey they’re wearing, but who is going to represent us,” Ratliff said.

Whitley concluded by encouraging voters to support Talarico, while Smith declared, “We need politicians that are going to bring us together, and that is James Talarico, and it certainly is not Ken Paxton.”

However, voting records obtained by Breitbart News show that some of the Republicans featured in Talarico’s advertisement have previously participated in Democratic primaries.

Former Republican Rep. Alan Steelman participated in Democratic primaries in both 2024 and 2026, while former State Rep. Todd Smith has voted Democrat in two of the last four elections.

On Friday, Talarico’s campaign released another endorsement video featuring former Republican State Rep. Jason Villalba, who previously supported Democrat Colin Allred’s unsuccessful 2024 Senate campaign against Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.

“I’m Jason Villalba. I’m a classic Ronald Reagan Republican, and I’m supporting James Talarico,” Villalba said.

“I got a chance to serve with some great men in the legislature. Ken Paxton was not one of them,” he continued.

“I think it’s important that we can trust our senator. We cannot have somebody in Washington that does not have the requisite character to represent Texans, and that is why I’m supporting James Talarico.”

“I’m not sure about you, but at our house, we don’t talk a lot about culture war issues because we’re more concerned about paying the bills,” he said. “Those kinds of arguments are meant to incite you to do certain things and vote certain ways. They’re not really based on facts.”

“Let’s make our decisions this time based on the issues that really matter. Let’s lower those grocery prices. Let’s lower that price of gas. Let’s get rid of these tariffs. Let’s get out of these wars,” he continued. “I know that’s what James talks about on the trail, and that certainly isn’t what Ken is talking about.”

In an October 2024 article titled “‘Republicans for Allred’ Coalition Stacked With Former GOP Losers,” Texas Scorecard reported that Villalba, Ratliff, and Smith were among the Republicans backing Democrat Colin Allred’s Senate campaign.

 The coalition was led by former Republican Rep. Adam Kinzinger, with Villalba serving as co-chair. Villalba lost his 2018 Republican primary and a 2019 Dallas mayoral bid, while Smith lost a state Senate race and Ratliff lost Republican primaries in 2014 and 2016. Kinzinger and other coalition members also endorsed Kamala Harris over Donald Trump in 2024.

Talarico’s campaign also previously highlighted support from three Texas women who identified themselves as Republicans, despite their histories of supporting Democratic candidates. The Daily Wire reported in August that former school board candidate Mindy McClure, who described herself as a “moderate Republican,” had donated to Democratic candidates and anti-Trump organizations through ActBlue dating back to 2018, including Kamala Harris’s 2024 presidential campaign and the Lincoln Project. Another participant, Erin Montgomery, had not voted in a Republican primary since at least 2017 and had participated in more Democratic than Republican primaries over the preceding two decades, according to a Republican source who reviewed voting records. 

A Talarico campaign spokesperson told Fox News the women had no official ties to the campaign, maintaining that Republicans were supporting Talarico over Ken Paxton. Meanwhile, former Tarrant County Judge Glen Whitley, featured in Talarico’s latest advertisement, previously endorsed Harris and Democrat Colin Allred in 2024.

A similar strategy has emerged in Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, where Democratic State Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott is challenging Republican Rep. Zach Nunn.

Trone Garriott appeared alongside a group of self-identified Republican supporters at a campaign event in Urbandale on Wednesday, emphasizing what her campaign characterized as bipartisan support.

“I voted for Zach Nunn last go-around and was very disappointed in promises unkept,” Lee Prince told KCCI.

“I am a lifelong Republican, but this year I’m voting for Sarah, and I’m encouraging all of you to vote for Sarah,” Roger Garrett said.

However, records obtained by Breitbart News show that Prince has not participated in a Republican primary since 2016 and previously contributed to Democratic presidential candidates Joe Biden and Pete Buttigieg.

Garrett, meanwhile, has an established history of financially supporting Trone Garriott dating back to 2020.

Campaign finance records show Garrett made four contributions to Trone Garriott totaling $350, including $100 on October 24, 2020; $150 on February 5, 2022; $50 on May 16, 2022; and another $50 on August 17, 2022.

The contributions suggest that Garrett’s support for Trone Garriott predates the current congressional contest by several years, rather than representing a newfound endorsement from a Republican voter.

Nunn, meanwhile, has also received crossover support from Democrats, including elected officials who publicly identify with the opposing party.

His campaign released an advertisement featuring Democratic Des Moines City Council members Mike Simonson and Joe Gatto, Clive City Council member Eric Klein, and victims’ rights advocate Tiffany Allison, who also identifies as a Democrat.

“I’m a moderate Democrat on Des Moines City Council,” Simonson said in the advertisement.

“I’m not voting for Sarah Trone Garriott,” Gatto said.

The advertisement’s narrator characterized Trone Garriott as “too extreme,” while Klein said, “She’s not for common sense solutions.”

“I’m voting for Zach Nunn,” Allison declared.

“I’m supporting Rob Sand, and I strongly support Zach Nunn,” Simonson said, referring to Iowa’s Democratic gubernatorial candidate.

“Zach Nunn delivers for Iowa,” Gatto said.

“Zach really cares. He’s fighting for all of us,” Allison added.

According to Axios Des Moines, Simonson and Gatto’s endorsements have drawn backlash from fellow Democrats, including a pledge to withdraw future financial support.

The report also noted that Simonson was previously listed among Trone Garriott’s local endorsements in December 2025 and donated $7,500 to her that year, illustrating his own shift in support.

Des Moines City Council member Carl Voss has also endorsed Trone Garriott.

“Republicans, Democrats, and Independents support Zach Nunn because they know he delivers for Iowa,” Nunn campaign spokesman Mark Matava told Axios.
news.summary:
Democratic U.S. Senate and House candidates in Texas and Iowa are highlighting endorsements from self-described Republicans in the final days before the midterm elections, but voting and campaign finance records obtained by Breitbart News reveal that several of those supporters have previously participated in Democratic primaries, donated to Democratic candidates, or publicly endorsed Democrats in earlier elections.

news.title: Elon Musk Warns 2028 Democratic Sweep Could Mean ‘End of Democracy’
news.text: Billionaire Elon Musk issued a stark warning to voters if Democrats sweep the chambers of Congress and the presidency in 2028, saying it could lead to the "end of democracy." Musk's message comes just four days ahead of the midterm elections, where Democrats are favored to take the House and face a competitive battle to flip the Senate. In his post to X early Friday morning, Musk laid out his three concerns. The first, he says, Democrats will make Puerto Rico and the District of Columbia states, in an effort to achieve a strong majority in the Senate. Secondly, Musk warned that Democrats would open the borders and "legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority." Lastly, Musk said Democrats would increase the size of the Supreme Court in an effort to gain an immediate majority. "This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word. All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029. That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election. Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one," Musk concluded in his post. Billionaire businessman Mark Cuban reacted to Musk's post on X saying: "I’m against all of these. The new force in politics and elections is independents. The fact independents are NOT an organized party, means we can individually do what we think is right, without regard to party politics. That is a force we have not seen before. And it is only growing as we all become increasingly disgusted by party politics. Pushing these would backfire on Democrats," Cuban said. This is not the first time the Tesla and SpaceX CEO has made a fourth quarter election warning. During the 2024 presidential election, Musk said that if President Donald Trump lost his race to then Vice President Kamala Harris, it would have been the last election for Americans due to immigration that would have turned the U.S. into a "single party country." Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have recently slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. The polling lows come as Trump has crisscrossed the country in the lead-up to November 3, to rally for potentially vulnerable GOP candidates. Newsweek reached out to the White House, Musk via SpaceX, and the Democratic National Committee (DNC) by email on Friday for comment. What Democrats Have Said About Supreme Court Justices and Puerto Rico, D.C. Statehood Musk is not the first person to raise the concern of Democrats potentially expanding the Supreme Court or pushing D.C. and Puerto Rican statehood over the finish line. In April, Trump ripped into longtime political commentator James Carville over the thoughts, saying in part, "Wacko James Carville, a so-called Democrat 'strategist,' wants the Democrats to make D.C. and Puerto Rico States and, most importantly, pack the Supreme Court, putting 13 Justices on the Court. Other Dems want 21 Justices. If they pull off adding these two States, these Country Destroying Sleazebags will dominate politics in America, if we even have a Nation left, for 100 years (TERMINATE THE FILIBUSTER!)." House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was asked if he supports adding more justices to the High Court earlier this year, and he responded saying that he supports reform. "What I support is dramatic reform, and what that looks like, to begin with, is making sure that the Supreme Court actually has an ethical code of conduct so that they’re not able to simply conduct themselves in ways that are inconsistent with the notion in this country that no one is above the law, " Jeffries said on NBC's Meet The Press in August. He added that Judiciary Committee Democrats will look further into what "dramatic reform" could be. Notably, Kamala Harris has previously supported the idea of adding justices to the Court and making D.C. and Puerto Rico states. “I believe that we need to expand the Supreme Court,” Harris said on the Baby, This is Keke Palmer podcast this month. “We need more justices on the Supreme Court so that we can have a court that actually reinforces the spirit and principles behind the Constitution of the United States.” She also supported pushing for Puerto Rico and D.C. statehood if their residents want it, during the podcast. Democratic Representative Jim Clyburn of South Carolina previously said he too would support adding seats to the High Court. Lawmakers recently voted on a GOP-backed amendment to cap the Supreme Court at nine justices. The vote failed to get two-thirds support. D. Stephen Voss, political professor at the University of Kentucky, told Newsweek on Friday in part, "Expanding the number of states in a way that would improve Democratic political fortunes has long been a goal among activists on the left, although it's unclear how broadly popular such proposals would be with mainstream Democratic politicians in Congress." Democrats and Immigration As Trump's second term is well underway, Democrats have made their opposition to his administration's immigration policies known. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids in major U.S. cities, deportations and fatal shootings involving federal agents have prompted Democrats to speak out in fury. Trump has made stricter border enforcement a key pillar of his presidency, including efforts to continue building a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border and initially suspending asylum at the border, which has faced legal setbacks. However, numerous Democrats, including candidates in key midterm races, have hit back at President Joe Biden's handling of the border, going as far as to say he "failed us." Democrats have also called for making the path to obtain U.S. citizenship simpler while leaning into ICE as a central focus of the midterms. Democratic candidates, like Florida's Angie Nixon and Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, have called for ICE to be abolished or dismantled while advocating for a new immigration enforcement system to be built "from scratch." On its website, the DNC says in part that the party believes in "secure borders, common-sense immigration laws, and fair enforcement." "We also believe in the humanity and dignity of every person. Federal agents should not be able to take over your city, target children, or kill innocent people in the streets," the DNC added on its website. Voss later said in his response to Newsweek that, "On the other hand, the Democratic Party has not advocated either throwing open the borders or granting widespread amnesty to illegal migrants. At worst, a critic might argue that today's Democratic Party opposes most muscular policies intended to curtail immigration." How Much Money Has Musk Donated This Midterm Cycle? Earlier this month, The New York Times reported that Musk spent $276 million, with a majority going to the Senate Leadership Fund, this cycle. He also donated $76 million earlier this year to his America PAC, which has backed Republicans in House and Senate races. On Friday, The Times reported the total figure of Musk's spending has risen to nearly $475 million this cycle. Newsweek cannot independently verify that figure at the time of publication. Other outlets also highlight that Musk's spending has surpassed $400 million. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Musk laid out his concerns if Democrats win the majority, while urging voters to back Republican senators in the midterms.

news.title: 'The View' co-hosts agree Democrats should not impeach Trump if party wins back control of Congress
news.text: "The View" co-hosts agreed with former Vice President Kamala Harris Friday that impeachment would not be a good use of the Democratic Party’s time and resources if the party wins back control of Congress in the midterm elections. "I think that going on in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea," Harris warned Tuesday on "The Parnas Perspective" podcast. "OK, just to be honest with you. Because we have limited resources, and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations. And that's where the time should be spent. Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-round and the votes aren't there, right? So, that's how I feel." After playing a clip of Harris' comments, "The View" co-hosts agreed with her assessment. KAMALA HARRIS BREAKS WITH LEFT FLANK, WARNS DEMS THAT IMPEACHING TRUMP IS 'NOT A GOOD IDEA' "In terms of Trump, no, I don't think that's what should be on the agenda," co-host Sunny Hostin said. "Hakeem Jeffries — who I believe will be the next speaker of the House, after November — he has a plan for 100 days which includes tax credits, taking care of the tax credits, limiting ICE and also stock trades. "And then he's got a plan for the first 100 hours, which would include, you know, just undoing a lot of unpopular Trump policies. So, I think there is a plan in place that Democrats have, and it may not include impeaching Trump." "I think that Democrats have to be realistic of what's achievable," co-host Ana Navarro said. "We are four days away from the election. So, before we start talking about what Democrats are going to do once they win, they've got to make sure they win. "People have to focus not on all of the conversation about impeachment and what is going to happen but rather on getting out the vote and getting people to the polls so that the American people decide who they want in power in the House and in the Senate. "There's a limit to what Democrats are going to be able to do even if they win the House, even if they win the House and the Senate, because Donald Trump is still president," she continued. "Legislation in this country needs to be signed by the president. If not, it needs to have a veto-proof majority. And I think that's going to be very difficult to achieve. I'm completely against impeachment. "There's 100 other ways to hold Donald Trump and his administration accountable," Navarro added. "Impeachment is an exercise that's moot if you don't have the 67 votes in the Senate required to indict." Joy Behar pointed to former President Richard Nixon's resignation from office after Republican lawmakers warned him that he lacked sufficient Senate support to avoid conviction if impeached and said of Trump, "If we don't have the votes to convict, there's no point in impeaching." DEM MAKING SENATE COMEBACK BID SAYS HE WOULDN'T SUPPORT A TRUMP IMPEACHMENT PUSH Sara Haines also agreed, arguing that many of Trump’s supporters are now angry with him for breaking campaign promises and that Democrats could capitalize on their dissatisfaction by delivering on their own promises. "It's important to recognize the moment," she said. "Donald Trump was elected and promised things he never touched. He's been remodeling, redecorating, working to revenge, all the things. The voters were left high and dry, which is why we're seeing some red states flip full to blue," she said. "That's why we are watching this campaigning. "They need to see someone get in there, hold them accountable, do the investigations, fine," Haines continued. "But really show the American people that what they promised, to fix all these things, that immediately there's action taken. Even if it can't get past the president. Spin the wheels. Show the people that you are putting up policy, that you are taking things to vote, that you are actually acting for the people that put you there." "Impeachment is not where the focus should be," Alyssa Farah Griffin said. "It costs actually a lot of money to do a trial, do the investigation. "What I think is important is there are day one things that would be beneficial for all Americans and a lot of Republicans would be on board with that a Democratic Congress could do," she continued. "Repealing Trump's tariffs, that is the power of the purse controlled by Congress and trying to wind down or pause the war in Iran. Those are things you should get Republican votes to do. That will bring down people's fuel prices. Those are where the focus should be." Earlier this month, veteran Democratic strategist James Carville also warned Democrats against impeaching Trump if the party wins control of Congress in the midterms. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Democratic strategist and co-host of "The Huddle" podcast Dan Turrentine told Fox News Digital, "Neither the Senate arithmetic nor the American people are there. Folks are angry with the president about the economy, tariffs, healthcare, the war with Iran, corruption. They feel he is focused on everything but them. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Our job is to fight for the real lives of real people, solving their problems, while providing appropriate oversight of the executive branch and trusting the electorate provides accountability," he added. "The quickest path back to the minority or continuing to be on the outside, looking into the White House, is to focus on revenge and score settling."
news.summary: Former Vice President Kamala Harris warned Democrats against impeaching President Donald Trump, and "The View" co-hosts agreed the focus should be on accountability and investigations.

news.title: Inside the Fight to Flip the Biggest Battleground in Texas
news.text:
I met up with Crystal Mason in mid-October, in a hilly neighborhood south of downtown Fort Worth. She was easy enough to recognize—she wore a black t-shirt with a pair of bright red boxing gloves on the front, and a single word in big block letters, “STILL ACQUITTED.” 

Eight years ago, amid a push by Texas Republican officials to find and prosecute instances of voter fraud, the Fort Worth resident was sentenced to five years in prison for voting in the 2016 presidential election while on supervised release for a felony conviction. Mason argued that she had never been informed she couldn’t vote, and that she cast only a provisional ballot, which was never counted. In 2024, a court agreed and threw out the conviction, but Tarrant County’s Republican district attorney appealed that decision. She finally beat the case for good this September—and then got right back to work. 

When I met her, she was checking a voter list on her phone and rattling off instructions to a group of volunteers—two daughters, a son, and one grandkid—who had accompanied her to knock doors and check in with residents on a 94-degree afternoon. These days, when she’s not driving a box truck for her day job, she runs a voting rights group called Crystal Mason: The Fight. In recent weeks she’d participated in registration drives, hit the doors, and stopped by a senior center on karaoke night to make sure voters there had a plan to get to the polls.

The kind of organizing Mason and others have been doing has taken on a new urgency ahead of the November election. In September, the Republican-led county commission eliminated 92 Election Day voting sites—nearly a third of its 2024 total. Advocates argued the reductions would disproportionately affect Black and Hispanic areas. Mason calls the closures “unreal.”

This would be a big deal anywhere, but Tarrant is not just any county; it’s the state’s ultimate battleground. The area has narrowly backed Democrats at the top of the ticket in some recent cycles, but it’s the last of the state’s big urban counties still run by Republicans—including the district attorney who tried to reinstate Mason’s conviction. And the conservative enclaves of Tarrant have played an outsized role in shaping the recent trajectory of the Texas Republican Party. This year’s Conservative Political Action Conference took place in the Fort Worth suburb of Grapevine. Bo French, the racist nominee for Texas Railroad Commission who wants to remove all Muslims from the United States, is a former Tarrant GOP chair. The True Texas Project, formerly known as the Northeast Tarrant Tea Party, celebrated its 15th anniversary by hosting a conversation on “the war on white America”; this fall, it’s held screenings of a new documentary called Don’t Sharia My Texas, at chapters around the state.

In light of the stakes and the preeminence of Tarrant County, the local Democratic Party headquarters in an office park on the edge of Fort Worth had been bustling with volunteers and candidates, as well as ink-stained wretches like me. When I spent a little too long admiring the political paraphernalia at the front of the office—including Kamala Harris-branded beer cans and a wine glass for Wendy Davis—Reyne Telles, the Tarrant County Democratic Party’s executive director, wistfully quoted the Boston Globe’s recent description of the space: “The Tarrant County Democratic Party office is a shrine to great hopes past.” 

Telles says that every statewide candidate on his side of the ledger has a number in mind for how much they need to win the county by in order to win the state—generally somewhere between three and eight percentage points. But there are some indications Democrats have made inroads, including with residents who traditionally support the other side. In a special election earlier this year, a Democratic union leader named Taylor Rehmet stunned political observers by flipping a state Senate district that had voted for Trump by 17 points. The data suggested he owed much of his success to persuasion, not turnout. While the official county Republican organization carries the flag for the far right, Fort Worth’s moderate Republican mayor, Mattie Parker, has endorsed Democratic candidates for two statewide offices—railroad commissioner (against French) and attorney general. Glen Whitley, who served for 16 years as Tarrant County judge (it’s the equivalent of county executive) cut an ad endorsing Democratic state Rep. James Talarico over Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in the race for US Senate. 

While Talarico and gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa have captured most of the headlines (guilty), the stakes are high in Tarrant County’s local races, where Democrats have not won a countywide race in decades. Alisa Simmons, a Democratic county commissioner, is in a tight race against the incumbent county judge Tim O’Hare—a conservative Bo French ally who pushed the reduction in polling locations. 

“He’s a really interesting person—I’m not sure why he even wanted to serve because he’s not serving,” Simmons told me, before a fundraiser at a private home in Colleyville.

Good governance has been a major feature of the campaign. In 2025, even before Republicans in the state legislature redrew the state’s congressional maps, O’Hare embarked on an unusual attempt to gerrymander the county commissioner districts, in order to secure what Republicans hope will be a 4–1 majority. The commission has cut its meeting schedule in half, all guest speakers are limited to one minute, and attendees have been hauled out by sheriffs deputies for clapping. (In one notable case, a local activist who used the word “bullshit” in his testimony was charged, one week later, with disorderly conduct.) In our short conversation, Simmons took aim at the county’s Republican leaders for cutting taxes meant to fund the county hospital, and highlighted the rising death toll at Tarrant County jails. 

“We almost rival Harris County, and Harris County is double the population,” she said, referring to the jurisdiction that includes Houston.

Democrats in Tarrant believe the county is there for the taking this year—that the apathy and resignation that have kept turnout lower than other large urban counties is changing, and that the Republicans on the ballot aren’t cut out for swing-state realities. Telles told me he hoped flipping the countywide races would send a signal to other corners of the state, that if a historically Republican metro famous for its cattle drives and western culture can vote blue, they can too. Republicans have pushed voter-fraud narratives and ruthless gerrymandering to preserve their grip on power. But in doing so, they also reminded voters what was really at stake.

As we walked through Fort Worth, I suggested to Mason that the kind of ordeal she went through might have easily turned her away from politics. 

“I realized that’s exactly what they wanted me to do,” she said. “And that was to stand on display and tell them how I would never vote again to discourage the black and the brown from coming to the polls.” She had an obligation, she said, “to make sure that I let them know that these same people that did this to me are elected officials.”

Mason’s door-knocking was a strictly nonpartisan operation. She congratulated a young woman who was preparing to vote for the first time, and double-checked that she knew which precinct to stop by. But not long after, voters in select Texas ZIP codes began seeing a new ad in which James Talarico sits at a kitchen table with a familiar voting-rights activist.

“Crystal didn’t back down,” he says.“And you shouldn’t either,” Mason tells the audience.

news.title: Karoline Leavitt joins Elon Musk pushing conspiracy about Supreme Court if Democrats win in the midterms
news.text:
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has joined MAGA figures in peddling Elon Musk’s conspiracy theories ahead of the midterms, including an alleged plot to change the Supreme Court that would render America a “permanent one-party state.”

As the polls are increasingly pointing to a Democratic blowout next week, Musk shared a post Friday on X listing his “biggest concern[s]” if Republicans lose control of the House, Senate, and White House in 2028. 

Musk claimed that if Democrats are successful, they will “increase the size of the Supreme Court to gain an immediate majority.” 

“This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word,” he claimed.

Leavitt, who left her White House role earlier this year to focus on her family, reshared the post to her Instagram stories and said, “This is what’s at stake. Vote.”

Some prominent Democrats have called for overhauling the Supreme Court, currently stacked in favor of the Republicans with a 6-3 conservative majority. 

For example, Rhode Island Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse proposed term limits for justices, and Rep. Jamie Raskin and former Vice President Kamala Harris have supported the idea of increasing the number of justices from nine to 13. If Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress, they could put four new justices on the court and swing the majority, if the numbers increase to 13. 

Supreme Court scholars have noted that reform is unlikely. The path to overhauling the highest court in the land is complex and would likely face enormous challenges, even if the Democrats retake the House and Senate next week.

The world’s richest man also claimed that if Democrats regain power, they will “make DC and Puerto Rico states to gain a strong majority in the Senate,” and “open the borders and legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority.”

He pushed the theories to warn his 241.5 million X followers that they could stop it from happening if they voted Republican on November 3. 

“All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029,” he said. “That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election.”

“It would be game over for America,” added Musk, who sewed chaos at the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term overseeing the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency.

Other MAGA figures jumped on his post and amplified it to their supporters.

“Pay attention folks,” said the president’s son, Don Jr. 

“The most important post in the history of X right here,” said conservative commentator Benny Johnson.

Former deputy FBI director Dan Bongino simply said: “Please Read This.” 

Katie Miller, married to deputy White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, also reshared Leavitt’s post.

In September, Republicans attempted to permanently limit the number of justices to nine but the amendment was struck down in the House.
news.summary: ‘It would be game over for America,’ said Musk, who sewed chaos overseeing the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency

news.title: Early voting jumps across Senate battlegrounds as millions more Americans vote ahead of Election Day
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Early voting is significantly outpacing the last midterm election, with millions more Americans casting ballots in advance and particularly sharp increases in states hosting competitive Senate races, according to an Associated Press analysis of voting data five days before Election Day.

The surge is especially pronounced in Texas, where voters are deciding closely watched Senate, House and governor's races. More than 6.3 million Texans had voted early as of Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point four years ago, a 50 percent increase.

Advance voting has also increased more than 30 percent from the same point four years ago in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, states with competitive Senate races. In South Carolina, where voters are choosing a successor to the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, early voting is up 83 percent.

Data comes 5 days before Election Day

The data, compiled by the AP, offers a glimpse of early voter participation five days before an election that will determine control of Congress and other key contests.

Across the country, more than 43 million Americans had voted early in person or returned mail ballots, nearly 10 million more than in 2022. The figures cover 47 states and Washington, D.C., compared with 48 states and the nation's capital four years ago.

In states that provide information on voters' party affiliation, about 6.8 million Democrats and 5.2 million Republicans have cast ballots early. Those figures do not account for all early voters nationwide or indicate which candidates received their votes.

The increase comes as voters prepare to decide control of Congress two years into President Donald Trump's second term, with Republicans holding the House and the Senate.

The turnout has been Texas-sized

Voters have turned out in droves during Texas' two-week early in-person voting period, which ends Friday.

In Harris County, which includes Houston, 862,700 people had voted as of Wednesday, compared with 564,500 at the same point in 2022.

The surge comes in a county that has reliably voted Democratic in recent elections, though by varying margins. In 2024, Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris defeated Trump by nearly 6 percentage points in the presidential contest, while Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred carried the county by roughly 11 percentage points over Republican Sen. Ted Cruz.

This year, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico in a closely watched Senate race, while Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is seeking reelection against Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Hundreds of millions of dollars have poured into the Senate race as Republicans fight to defend a state where Democrats have not won a statewide election in more than three decades. Trump visited Texas earlier this week, his third trip to the state in a month.

Early voting surges across Senate battleground states

Republicans are defending a 53-47 Senate majority in a midterm election in which the battleground map has expanded significantly, with Democrats hoping to pull off upsets in states that have long favored Republicans.

In South Carolina, where Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024, early voting has surged 83 percent compared with the same point in 2022. The state has open races for governor and U.S. Senate this year.

In Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces Democratic Methodist megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, early voting has increased 34 percent, with roughly 83,000 more ballots cast than at the same point four years ago.

Michigan and Maine, both of which have closely watched Senate races, are also seeing increases.

In Maine, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins faces Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson, early voting is up 44 percent. Michigan has recorded roughly 409,000 more early votes than at the same point in 2022, a 32 percent increase.

Voters in Michigan approved early in-person voting in November 2022, making this the first midterm election in which it is available statewide.

Best I can tell, all of this really started in May when Harris first mentioned packing the Court, though she's not alone in this.

Spurred by the Supreme Court’s recent racial redistricting decision, important Democrats are once again calling for court packing if their party can run the table in 2028.Kamala Harris, the failed 2024 presidential nominee but an early front-runner in the next race according to several polls, flirted with the court-packing club on Friday. Talking election strategy last week with a left-wing nonprofit, she urged “Supreme Court reform, including the notion of expanding the court.”James Carville, a longtime Democratic adviser and strategist, may be the most enthusiastic backer of the idea. “If the Democrats win the presidency and both houses of Congress,” he said on his podcast last month, “I think on day one, they should make Puerto Rico, D.C. a state, and they should expand the Supreme Court to 13. Fuck it, eat our dust.”Thirteen is the magic number for Democratic court packers, because they need to add four new liberal justices to beat the current 6–3 conservative majority. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries seems to be on board. “We’re gonna have to do something about the Supreme Court,” said Jeffries. “And let me be very clear: Everything is on the table—everything—to deal with this corrupt MAGA majority that is issuing political opinions that are designed to bolster the prospects of the Republican Party.”Rep. Rashida Tlaib was more direct: “Impeach these corrupt justices. Expand the Court.” Also piling on was left-wing influencer and former MSNBC host Mehdi Hasan, telling his 2 million X followers: “If the Democrats don’t make rebalancing and expanding the Supreme Court a top priority for whenever (if?) they next get into power, then I don’t know what to say anymore.”

Democrats can't pack the Court without at least 60 votes in the Senate and control of the White House. So this really isn't on the horizon anytime soon. But I guess you could see it as a swing-for-the-fences approach to the 2028 campaign. Then again, if they nuke the filibuster, it would be easier. That's probably how to take these calls to pack the Court. They are planning to take extreme measures so they can take even more extreme measures.

But obviously Democrats would be making a big mistake to think that Republicans will never again be in power. If it happens, they too could pack the court. I think that's why part of this is adding two new states and getting rid of the electoral college. Democrats need to backstop this power grab by making sure Republicans never hold the Senate again. And if they never hold the Senate (or the White House thanks to some kind of national popular vote election) then they can never undo or expand the court themselves.

The plan is to save democracy by effectively ending the ability of one of the two parties to compete. That's what Harris is really saying, though I doubt she's thought about it beyond memorizing the talking points given to her by some staffer.

Still, the fact that she could be the 2028 front-runner and she's already putting this out there now is worrisome. The Democrat Party continues to run to the far left as fast as it can.
